answer.actor: A blind man who reviewed mishnayot before Mar Shmuel
answer.event: The blind man was late one day; Mar Shmuel sent a messenger to his house, who missed him on the road and on returning reported that the blind man's wife had committed adultery.
answer.turn: A lone witness accuses the wife, and the blind man must decide whether to act on it.
answer.outcome: Mar Shmuel told him to divorce her if he trusted the messenger, and not to divorce her otherwise.
answer.summary: A blind man used to review mishnayot before Mar Shmuel. One day he was late, so Mar Shmuel sent a messenger to fetch him; the two took different roads and missed each other. The messenger came back saying he had seen the man's wife committing adultery. The blind man asked Mar Shmuel what to do, and was told: if you trust this messenger, divorce her; if not, do not.

answer.event: Sages asked Rabbi Yehoshua whether the rival wife of a daughter is exempt, and pressed him for whose view is the halakha.
answer.turn: He refused to rule between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, saying he feared they would break his skull.
answer.outcome: Instead he testified that two great Jerusalem families descended from rival wives and produced High Priests.
answer.summary: Sages asked Rabbi Yehoshua about the law of a daughter's rival wife. He said it was disputed between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, and when pressed for the ruling he asked why they were putting his head between two great mountains, fearing they would crush his skull. Instead he offered testimony that two great Jerusalem families descended from such rival wives and produced High Priests.
answer.missing: The exchange is mostly a halakhic question and answer; there is little event beyond the refusal and testimony.

answer.actor: Rav Huna and his son Rabba
answer.event: Rav Huna tore silk garments in front of his son Rabba to test whether he would become angry.
answer.turn: The test of the son's restraint in honoring his father.
answer.summary: Rav Huna wanted to see whether his son Rabba would honor him even under provocation, so he tore expensive silk garments in front of him. The Gemara discusses how this could be permitted, explaining that Rav Huna had forgone his honor in advance.
answer.missing: The text does not say how Rabba reacted; the rest is legal discussion of the test.

answer.actor: Mar Yehuda and the residents of Mavrakhta
answer.event: Mar Yehuda found the residents of Mavrakhta placing their eiruv in the synagogue of Beit Agovar and told them to place it farther in to gain more distance.
answer.turn: Rava rebuked him, calling him argumentative.
answer.outcome: Rava declared that in eiruv matters no one follows Rabbi Akiva's opinion, so his advice was unnecessary.
answer.summary: Mar Yehuda came upon the people of Mavrakhta depositing their eiruv in the Beit Agovar synagogue and advised them to put it deeper inside so their Shabbat limit would extend farther. Rava scolded him as quarrelsome, saying that in eiruv law nobody follows Rabbi Akiva's view on which his advice depended.

answer.missing: This describes Rava's habitual practice when such cases came before him, not a single event.

answer.actor: Ravina, in the presence of Rav Ashi
answer.event: While sitting before Rav Ashi, Ravina saw a man tying his donkey to a palm tree on Shabbat, shouted at him, was ignored, and declared the man excommunicated.
answer.turn: Ravina worried that he had acted irreverently by ruling in his teacher's presence.
answer.outcome: Rav Ashi reassured him that where God's name is desecrated, no deference is owed even to a teacher.
answer.summary: Ravina was sitting before his teacher Rav Ashi when he saw a man tie his donkey to a palm tree on Shabbat. Ravina shouted at him, but the man ignored him, so Ravina pronounced him excommunicated. Afterward he asked Rav Ashi whether this had been disrespectful to him, and Rav Ashi answered that where God's name is being desecrated, one does not defer to one's teacher.

answer.event: Ravin went as an agent to betroth a woman for his son but betrothed her to himself.
answer.turn: The woman's family would not give her to the son, and Ravin feared someone else would betroth her while he went to report back.
answer.outcome: He married her himself.
answer.summary: Ravin the Pious set out to arrange a betrothal for his son, but ended up betrothing the woman to himself. The Gemara explains that her family refused to give her to the son, and that Ravin did not first tell his son because he feared that in the meantime someone else would betroth her.

answer.missing: A case of betrothal with silk is cited only as the occasion for a legal dispute between Rabba and Rav Yosef; no narrative.

answer.actor: Rav Yosef and his student Abaye
answer.event: Rav Yosef, having forgotten his learning, said he had never heard a teaching, and Abaye reminded him that he himself had taught it to them.
answer.turn: Rav Yosef recalled the teaching but in a different form than Abaye reported it.
answer.outcome: Rav Yosef restated what he had actually taught, reconciling Abaye's mention of residents.
answer.summary: Rav Yosef said he had never heard a certain ruling of Shmuel about adjacent roofs. His student Abaye told him that he had taught it to them himself, and repeated it. Rav Yosef then remembered and corrected Abaye's version, explaining what he had really said.
answer.missing: The forgetting is implied rather than told; most of the exchange is the content of the halakha.

answer.event: In a good mood, Rava boasted that he was like ben Azzai ready to answer any question, and a Sage asked him how many apples are needed for an eiruv.
answer.turn: Rava answered that one cannot make an eiruv with apples, and the Sage cited a mishna implying that one can.
answer.summary: Rava, feeling sharp, declared himself like ben Azzai in the markets of Tiberias, ready for any question. One of the Sages tested him by asking how many apples make an eiruv. Rava replied that apples cannot be used, and the Sage challenged him from a mishna saying all foods combine for an eiruv.
answer.missing: How Rava answered the challenge and how the exchange ended.

answer.event: A ritual bath in Yavne presumed full was measured and found deficient, and Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva disputed the status of purifications done in it.
answer.turn: After an exchange of parables, Rabbi Akiva produced an argument distinguishing the cases.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Tarfon conceded, praising Akiva: whoever separates from you separates from life.
answer.summary: A ritual bath in Yavne thought to hold the required amount was measured and found short. Rabbi Tarfon held that everything purified in it remained pure, while Rabbi Akiva held it impure, and they argued through parables about priests found disqualified. Rabbi Akiva showed that the bath's flaw was like a blemished priest's, and Rabbi Tarfon accepted it, telling Akiva that leaving him is like leaving life.

answer.event: Rabbi Elazar ascended to Eretz Yisrael, was ordained, and was appointed to the council for intercalating the calendar.
answer.turn: At each step he declared he had escaped one more of the curses Ezekiel pronounced on false prophets.
answer.outcome: He had been spared all three curses.
answer.summary: When Rabbi Elazar went up to the Land of Israel, he said he had escaped one curse. When he was ordained, he said two, and when he was seated on the calendar council, three. He was referring to Ezekiel's curse that false prophets would not enter the land, be written in Israel's register, or sit in God's council.

answer.missing: Only a bare mention that Abaye and Rava disputed a balcony all their lives, cited as legal proof.

answer.event: Rav came to Apsetaya and forbade its residents to climb even a stripped tree on Shabbat.
answer.turn: He found the place lax in observance and added a protective stringency.
answer.outcome: The stricter rule was imposed there.
answer.summary: Rav visited Apsetaya and prohibited the people from climbing even a tree stripped of its branches on Shabbat. The Gemara explains that this was not the basic law: he found the place neglectful and built a fence around it.
answer.missing: The episode is cited briefly as a legal precedent; no reaction or aftermath is told.

answer.event: At his son's wedding Rava served drinks; two Sages stood for him and two did not.
answer.turn: Rava became angry at those who did not stand.
answer.outcome: He rebuked them, asking whether they alone were Sages and the others not.
answer.summary: Rava poured drinks for the guests at his son's wedding. Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua stood when he approached, but Rav Mari and Rav Pinehas son of Rav Hisda did not. Rava was offended and asked sharply whether those two thought themselves Sages and the others not.

answer.actor: Mar Yehuda, Rav Yosef and Rav Shmuel son of Rabba bar bar Hana, and Rabba
answer.event: Mar Yehuda found the two scholars at the door of Rabba's study hall and posed a contradiction between two baraitot about Rabbi Shimon.
answer.turn: They were silent and had no answer, so they went to Rabba.
answer.outcome: Rabba told them a quarrelsome person had put them up to it and resolved the contradiction.
answer.summary: Mar Yehuda met Rav Yosef and Rav Shmuel son of Rabba bar bar Hana at the entrance to Rabba's study hall and challenged them with two seemingly contradictory teachings of Rabbi Shimon. They could not answer and fell silent. They brought the question to Rabba, who said an argumentative person had set them up and explained that one teaching dealt with an animal found to be a tereifa.

answer.event: Rabbi Zeira avoided his teacher Rav Yehuda because he wanted to move to Eretz Yisrael and Rav Yehuda held that doing so violated a commandment.
answer.summary: Rabbi Zeira wanted to go up to the Land of Israel, but his teacher Rav Yehuda taught that leaving Babylonia for Israel transgresses a commandment. So Rabbi Zeira kept out of his teacher's sight.
answer.missing: What happened next: whether he left, met Rav Yehuda, or how it ended.

answer.event: Rabbi Hanina regularly sent four dinars to a pauper each Shabbat eve; one day he sent them with his wife.
answer.turn: She came back saying the man did not need charity, having overheard his household asked whether he dined on silver or gold tablecloths.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Hanina responded by quoting Rabbi Elazar that we should be grateful to swindlers, since they excuse our failures toward the truly poor.
answer.summary: Rabbi Hanina used to send a poor man four dinars every Friday. Once he sent his wife with the money, and she returned saying the man did not need it: she had heard people in his house asking whether he would dine on silver or gold tablecloths. Rabbi Hanina answered with Rabbi Elazar's saying that we should thank the swindlers, because without them we would be sinning every day by neglecting the poor.

answer.actor: A man from Shot Mishot and Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha
answer.event: A man told the Sages he came from Shot Mishot, and Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha stood and declared that the place lies between the rivers.
answer.turn: The declaration implied the man's lineage was as sound as that of the exile community.
answer.summary: A man told the Sages he was from Shot Mishot. Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha rose and announced that Shot Mishot is between the rivers, a region whose families count as having good lineage.
answer.missing: The text moves into legal geography; it does not say what became of the man.

answer.event: Rabbi Akiva picked an etrog on the first of Shevat and separated two tithes from it.
answer.turn: He tithed it according to both Beit Shammai's and Beit Hillel's dating of the new year for trees.
answer.summary: Rabbi Akiva picked an etrog on the first of Shevat. Unsure which year's tithing rules applied, he separated two tithes, one according to Beit Shammai and one according to Beit Hillel.
answer.missing: A single act cited as legal proof; no turn or consequence is told.

answer.event: Rabbi Zakkai recited a baraita before Rabbi Yochanan classifying the area between the side posts and beneath the cross beam as a karmelit.
answer.turn: Rabbi Yochanan rejected the teaching.
answer.outcome: He told Rabbi Zakkai to go and teach it outside the study hall.
answer.summary: Rabbi Zakkai recited a teaching before Rabbi Yochanan: the area between the side posts and under the cross beam of an alleyway has the status of a karmelit, where carrying is forbidden. Rabbi Yochanan dismissed it, telling him to go out and teach it outside, meaning it did not belong in the study hall.

answer.actor: Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
answer.event: Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua found the Sages in Rav's study hall arguing that halla is a Torah obligation today even if teruma is rabbinic.
answer.turn: He told them the opposite: even if teruma is Torah law, halla is rabbinic, citing a baraita about 'when you come into the land'.
answer.outcome: His argument concludes that in Ezra's time not all the people ascended, so halla was not restored as a Torah obligation; no reaction from the Sages is told.
answer.summary: Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua recounts that he came upon the Sages in Rav's study hall, who were saying that halla is a Torah obligation today even if teruma is not. He countered that the reverse holds, because the obligation applies only when all of Israel enters the land, and in Ezra's day not everyone came up. The incident is only a frame for a legal argument.
answer.missing: Any reaction or resolution from the Sages; the content is legal argument rather than events.

answer.actor: A man in Mata Mehasya and his brother
answer.event: A man whose brother died faced levirate marriage with the widow, and his brother wanted to disqualify her from him by giving her a bill of divorce.
answer.turn: The man offered to share the estate; the brother feared being cheated as the Pumbedita swindler had done, so the man offered to let him take his share immediately.
answer.outcome: The passage ends with the offer; whether the brother accepted or what happened is not told.
answer.summary: In Mata Mehasya a man was due to take his late brother's widow in levirate marriage, but another brother wanted to disqualify her by divorce. The man asked why, and offered to split the dead brother's property. The brother said he feared being swindled as the Pumbedita trickster had done, so the man offered to let him take his share right away.
answer.missing: The outcome: whether the offer was accepted and the levirate marriage went ahead.

answer.actor: A man who sold land to Rav Pappa
answer.event: A man sold land to Rav Pappa because he needed money to buy oxen.
answer.turn: In the end he did not need the money.
answer.outcome: Rav Pappa returned the land to him, which the Gemara says was beyond the letter of the law.
answer.summary: A man sold a field to Rav Pappa to raise money for oxen. When it turned out he no longer needed the money, Rav Pappa gave him back his land. The Gemara notes that Rav Pappa did this out of generosity, beyond what the law required.

answer.actor: The people of the Upper Galilee and a poor man of noble descent from Tzippori
answer.event: The people of the Upper Galilee bought a poor man of good family a litra of meat every day.
answer.summary: The people of the Upper Galilee provided a poor man of noble family from Tzippori with a litra of meat every day. The Gemara explains why this was remarkable: it was costly poultry, or they paid a litra of coins, or, as Rav Ashi says, in their small village they slaughtered a whole animal each day just for him.
answer.missing: A turn or ending; this describes an ongoing practice of charity rather than an event that develops.

answer.event: A sharecropper betrothed a woman with a handful of onions taken from the field he worked.
answer.turn: When he came before Rava, Rava asked who had given him the onions, meaning they were stolen.
answer.outcome: The betrothal was invalid; the Gemara adds that with a whole bundle it would have been different.
answer.summary: A sharecropper used a handful of onions from his landlord's field to betroth a woman, then came to Rava about it. Rava asked him who had allowed him to take them: the onions were not his, so the betrothal did not take effect. The Gemara notes that a whole bundle would be different, since he could claim it as his share of the crop.

answer.event: According to the judges of Pumbedita, Rav Yehuda decided a case involving bundles of vine branches.
answer.summary: The judges of Pumbedita reported that Rav Yehuda once ruled in a case about bundles of vine branches. The text gives only the bare report, and then ties it to his general view that eating even forbidden produce from land counts as taking possession of it.
answer.missing: The facts of the case and the ruling itself; the Hebrew gives only that he acted in a case of bundles of branches (the translation supplies the details).

answer.event: People came before Rabbi Ami with a bill of divorce that needed more witnesses.
answer.outcome: He told them to go and complete it even with a slave from the marketplace.
answer.summary: A case was brought to Rabbi Ami about a bill of divorce that lacked enough witnesses. He told them to go and complete the signatures even with a slave picked up from the market.
answer.missing: The details of who came and why; the Hebrew says only 'when they came before Rabbi Ami' (the translation supplies the case).

answer.actor: Rabbi Tarfon, Rabbi Akiva and the Elders
answer.event: Rabbi Tarfon and the Elders, reclining in the upper room of the house of Nitza in Lod, were asked whether study or action is greater.
answer.turn: Rabbi Tarfon said action, Rabbi Akiva said study.
answer.outcome: All agreed that study is greater because study leads to action.
answer.summary: Rabbi Tarfon and the Elders were gathered in an upper room in Lod when someone asked them whether study or action is greater. Rabbi Tarfon answered action; Rabbi Akiva answered study. In the end they all agreed that study is greater, because study leads to action.

answer.event: Ben Nappaha owned houses in five courtyards in Usha.
answer.turn: The case came before the Sages to decide whether all of them restricted carrying.
answer.outcome: The Sages ruled that only his place of residence renders carrying prohibited.
answer.summary: Rabbi Yehuda tells of ben Nappaha, who had houses in five courtyards in Usha. The question of whether each of them affected carrying in its courtyard came before the Sages. They ruled that only the place where he actually lived made carrying without an eiruv forbidden.

answer.actor: Rav Yosef, Abaye, and a daughter seeking support
answer.event: Someone came before Rav Yosef about a daughter's sustenance from her late father's estate, and he told the sons to give it to her from the dates on the drying mats.
answer.turn: Abaye objected that not even a creditor could collect from orphans' movable property.
answer.outcome: Rav Yosef clarified that he meant dates still on the tree, fit for the mats, and when pressed further, dates that still needed the palm, so they counted as land.
answer.summary: A case came to Rav Yosef about a daughter who needed support from her dead father's estate, and he told the heirs to give her from the dates laid out on mats. Abaye challenged him: would he let even a creditor collect from orphans' movable goods like that? Rav Yosef explained he meant dates ripe enough for the mats but still attached, and when Abaye pressed again, dates that still needed the tree, which count as land rather than movables.

answer.actor: Rav Mordekhai, Mar bar Rav Ashi, and Rav Ashi
answer.event: A dispute over whether a child's gift is valid was sent to Rav Mordekhai with the attributions reversed, so that Mar bar Rav Ashi seemed to say it is not valid.
answer.turn: Rav Mordekhai recalled that Rav Ashi, Mar's father, standing with one foot on the ground and one on the step, had ruled the child's gift valid.
answer.outcome: He sent back word to Mar bar Rav Ashi that the gift is valid in every case, large or small, deathbed or healthy.
answer.summary: Rav Yeimar and Mar bar Rav Ashi disagreed about whether a young child's gift is valid, but the report reached Rav Mordekhai with their names reversed. Rav Mordekhai sent word to Mar bar Rav Ashi reminding him of what had happened: his father Rav Ashi, standing with one foot on the ground and one on the step, was asked the question and answered that such a gift is valid in all cases.

answer.event: A woman seized a silver cup as partial payment of her marriage contract and also demanded sustenance.
answer.turn: She came before Rava for judgment.
answer.outcome: Rava told the orphans to give her sustenance, disregarding Rabbi Shimon's view that partial payment counts as full.
answer.summary: A widow took a silver cup toward her marriage settlement and still demanded to be supported from the estate. She brought the case to Rava, who told her late husband's orphans to go and give her sustenance, since no one follows Rabbi Shimon's view on this point.

answer.actor: Rabbi Hanina Kara and Rabbi Yannai
answer.event: Rabbi Hanina Kara sat before Rabbi Yannai and declared that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda.
answer.turn: Rabbi Yannai rejected the ruling.
answer.outcome: He told him to go out and recite his verses outside, since the halakha is not like Rabbi Yehuda.
answer.summary: Rabbi Hanina the Bible reciter was sitting before Rabbi Yannai and announced that the law follows Rabbi Yehuda. Rabbi Yannai sent him out, telling him to go recite his verses outside, because the law does not follow Rabbi Yehuda.

answer.event: Rav arrived at the house of bar Shafei Halla and examined the family.
answer.summary: Rav once visited the family of bar Shafei Halla and had them examined. The Gemara cites this only to ask what he was examining, and answers that he told people to check whether the family would fall silent in a quarrel, a sign of good lineage.
answer.missing: What the examination found and how the visit ended; the incident is only cited in a legal question.

answer.actor: Ravina and his host in Mehoza
answer.event: Ravina came to Mehoza, and his host showed him a slaughtering knife; Ravina told him to take it to Rava.
answer.turn: The host objected that Rava himself says a scholar may examine a knife for himself.
answer.outcome: Ravina answered that since he was only buying the meat, it did not count as slaughtering for himself.
answer.summary: Ravina visited Mehoza, Rava's town, and his host showed him a knife to check before slaughtering. Ravina told him to take it to Rava. The host asked whether Ravina did not accept Rava's rule that a scholar may check a knife for himself; Ravina replied that he was only buying meat from the host, so the rule did not apply.

answer.actor: The people of Neharde'a, and Rav Nahman
answer.event: During a drought in Neharde'a everyone sold their mansions to buy wheat.
answer.turn: In the end wheat arrived and the sales proved unnecessary.
answer.outcome: Rav Nahman ruled that the mansions return to their owners.
answer.summary: A drought struck Neharde'a and everyone sold their mansions to buy food. Then a wheat shipment arrived, and the sales turned out to have been needless. Rav Nahman ruled that by law the houses went back to their original owners.

answer.event: Rav Ashi visited Rav Kahana's house for a wedding and recited the wedding blessings over the following days.
answer.turn: After the first day he recited all seven blessings only when new faces were present; otherwise he treated it as a continuation of the celebration and said only two.
answer.summary: Rav Ashi came to Rav Kahana's house during a wedding celebration. On the first day he recited all seven wedding blessings. On later days he recited all of them only if new guests had come; otherwise he said just the blessing 'In Whose dwelling is joy' and 'Who has created', since it was merely an extension of the celebration.
answer.missing: The passage describes his practice over several days rather than a single turning point or ending.

answer.event: The two schools disputed for two and a half years whether it is better for man to have been created or not.
answer.turn: They took a vote.
answer.outcome: They concluded it would have been better for man not to have been created, but now that he exists he should examine his deeds.
answer.summary: For two and a half years the schools of Shammai and Hillel argued whether it would have been better for humanity never to have been created. Finally they took a vote and decided it would have been better not to be created. Since man has been created, however, he should examine his actions.
answer.missing: The dispute is reported as a debate and verdict, without any particular scene or actors.

answer.actor: A dying man, his daughter and heirs; Rav Ashi
answer.event: A man willed a palm tree to his daughter but left only two half-shares of palm trees, which the heirs wanted to give her.
answer.turn: Rav Ashi was unsure whether two halves of palm trees count as 'a palm tree'.
answer.outcome: Rav Mordekhai cited Rava that people do call two halves a palm tree, so the heirs could give her the two halves.
answer.summary: A man wrote in his will that his daughter should get a palm tree, but when he died he owned only half-shares in two trees. The heirs wanted to give her the two halves. Rav Ashi wondered whether two half-trees really count as 'a palm tree'; Rav Mordekhai told him, in Rava's name, that people do speak that way, so the halves sufficed.

answer.event: Villagers asked Rabbi Yirmeya whether an eiruv may be made with moist beans.
answer.turn: He did not know the answer.
answer.outcome: Back at the study hall he was told Rabbi Yannai permitted it, with Rav Yehiel giving the amount as a handful.
answer.summary: Rabbi Yirmeya visited some villages, and the people asked him whether they could make an eiruv with moist beans. He had no answer. When he returned to the study hall, the scholars told him Rabbi Yannai had ruled it permitted, and Rav Yehiel said a handful is needed.

answer.event: He performed a halitza with a non-leather slipper, alone as sole judge, at night.
answer.turn: Shmuel criticized him for relying on individual minority opinions.
answer.outcome: Shmuel's sarcastic rebuke stands as the verdict on his conduct.
answer.summary: Rabba bar Hiyya from Ctesiphon conducted a halitza ceremony using a slipper rather than a leather shoe, as the only judge, and at night. Shmuel scoffed at him, saying how bold he was to follow individual opinions not accepted as law.

answer.actor: Rav Aha bar Abba and Rav Hisda
answer.event: Rav Aha bar Abba visited his son-in-law Rav Hisda and sat his granddaughter on his lap.
answer.turn: Rav Hisda objected that she might be betrothed; they traded accusations of violating rulings of Rav and Shmuel.
answer.outcome: Rav Aha answered that he follows Shmuel's other ruling: all is permitted for the sake of Heaven.
answer.summary: Rav Aha bar Abba came to visit his son-in-law Rav Hisda and put his granddaughter on his lap. Rav Hisda asked whether he didn't think she might already be betrothed. Rav Aha retorted that betrothing a minor daughter would itself break Rav's ruling; Rav Hisda answered that holding a woman breaks Shmuel's ruling. Rav Aha replied that he follows another teaching of Shmuel: everything done for the sake of Heaven is permitted.

answer.event: The people of the Galilee asked Rabbi Helbo who reads from the Torah after the priest and Levite.
answer.turn: He did not know the answer.
answer.outcome: He asked Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha, who gave the order: scholars who are communal leaders, then scholars fit to lead, then their sons, then synagogue heads and anyone.
answer.summary: The Galileans sent Rabbi Helbo a question: after the priest and Levite, who should be called to the Torah? He did not know, so he went and asked Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha. Rabbi Yitzhak told him the order: scholars appointed as community leaders, then scholars fit to be appointed, then sons of such leaders, then heads of synagogues and finally anyone.

answer.actor: Ameimar, a woman and her brothers (reported by Rav Minyumi)
answer.event: A woman came before Ameimar claiming a tenth of her father's estate.
answer.turn: Her brothers said that if they had money they would pay her off in cash, and Ameimar said nothing against it.
answer.outcome: His silence showed he had come to regard a daughter as a creditor who can be paid in cash, retracting his earlier view.
answer.summary: Rav Minyumi recalled standing before Ameimar when a woman came asking for a tenth of her father's estate as her dowry. Her brothers told her that if they had the money they would simply pay her off in cash. Ameimar remained silent and did not object, which Rav Minyumi took as a sign that Ameimar had changed his mind and now treated the daughter as a creditor rather than an heir.

answer.actor: A half-slave half-free woman and her master
answer.event: The court forced the master of a half-slave half-free woman to free her.
answer.outcome: He emancipated her.
answer.summary: A woman who was half slave and half free was in a situation where the court compelled her master to set her fully free, and he did so. The Gemara then debates why: either because women are obligated to procreate, or because men were taking liberties with her.
answer.missing: The reason for the coercion is not stated in the incident itself; it is only argued about afterward.

answer.event: A man passed by the entrance of his father-in-law's house and Rav Sheshet had him lashed.
answer.turn: It is explained that the man was suspected of an affair with his mother-in-law.
answer.outcome: He was flogged.
answer.summary: A man merely passed by the door of his father-in-law's house, and Rav Sheshet had him flogged. The reason was that the man was rumored to be involved with his mother-in-law, so even passing near the house lent credence to the rumor.
answer.missing: The incident is cited briefly inside a legal argument; the explanation is the Gemara's, not part of a told scene.

answer.event: In a case where a creditor forgave a sold debt, Rafram pressed Rav Ashi to rule.
answer.turn: Rav Ashi ruled the creditor liable for indirect damage.
answer.outcome: He made the creditor pay the full value of the note.
answer.summary: A case came up in which a creditor voided a promissory note he had sold. Rafram pressed Rav Ashi to give a definite ruling, and Rav Ashi made the creditor pay the full amount of the debt, as if he had destroyed a valuable beam meant for a sculpture.
answer.missing: The facts of the case are given only by reference to the preceding legal discussion.

answer.actor: A yevama and yavam; Rabbi Akiva
answer.event: A couple performed halitza privately in prison, and the case came before Rabbi Akiva, who was imprisoned.
answer.turn: The question is how anyone knew what happened between them; witnesses watched from outside.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Akiva validated the halitza.
answer.summary: A man and woman performed halitza by themselves while in prison, and the case was brought to Rabbi Akiva, who was himself imprisoned. He validated it. The Gemara explains that witnesses had watched from outside, and that both the ceremony and the ruling took place in prison.
answer.missing: The incident itself is in the Mishna, which is only referred to, not shown.

answer.event: Rabbi went to study Torah with Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua.
answer.turn: The students ganged up on him like aggressive roosters and would not let him learn.
answer.outcome: He learned only one teaching: Rabbi Eliezer's ruling that intercourse with a hermaphrodite incurs stoning as with a male.
answer.summary: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi recalled going to study with Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua. The other students banded together against him like the fierce roosters of Beit Bukya and would not let him study there. In the end he came away with only one teaching from the Mishna: Rabbi Eliezer's ruling about a hermaphrodite.

answer.actor: Rav Yosef son of Rav Menashya of Dabil; Shmuel
answer.event: Rav Yosef ruled in a betrothal case following Rav rather than Shmuel.
answer.turn: Shmuel took offense and sarcastically asked whether this scholar had been given a bigger measure of wisdom than everyone else.
answer.summary: Rav Yosef of Dabil ruled in an actual case according to Rav's view, disregarding the father's betrothal. Shmuel was offended and sarcastically remarked that wisdom seems to have been measured out to everyone in a small measure but to this man in a large one.
answer.missing: The facts of the case and any resolution are not told; the incident is cited as evidence in an argument.

answer.actor: Rava and Rav Natan bar Ami
answer.event: Rava compelled the wealthy Rav Natan bar Ami to give charity.
answer.outcome: Rava collected four hundred zuz from him for charity.
answer.summary: Rava forced Rav Natan bar Ami, a wealthy man, to contribute to charity and took four hundred zuz from him for that purpose.
answer.missing: No circumstances or reaction are given; it is a bare report cited as precedent.

answer.event: A childless woman came before Rabbi Ami demanding her marriage-contract payment and a divorce.
answer.turn: He told her she was not commanded to have children; she answered that she needed children to care for her in old age.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Ami ruled that in such a case the husband is forced to divorce her.
answer.summary: A woman whose husband could not father children came to Rabbi Ami and asked for her marriage-contract money. He sent her away, saying women are not commanded to have children. She replied: who will care for this woman in her old age? Persuaded, Rabbi Ami ruled that in such a case the husband must be compelled to divorce her.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya and a heretic
answer.event: A heretic mocked Rabbi Yehoshua as a 'man of thorns', citing Micah's 'the best of them is as a brier'.
answer.turn: Rabbi Yehoshua called him a fool and pointed to the end of the verse.
answer.outcome: He reinterpreted the verse as praise: the righteous protect Israel like a thorn hedge, or crush the nations.
answer.summary: A heretic taunted Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya, calling him a 'man of thorns' because the prophet says the best of Israel are like briers. Rabbi Yehoshua called him a fool and told him to read the rest of the verse. He explained that the verse is praise: just as thorns seal a breach, the best among Israel protect it.

answer.event: A student of Rabbi Eliezer became liable to death by burning for his sins.
answer.turn: The Sages said to leave him alone because he had served a great man.
answer.outcome: He was spared.
answer.summary: One of Rabbi Eliezer's students committed a sin deserving death by burning. The Sages decided to leave him unpunished, because he had served a great teacher.
answer.missing: What he did and what happened afterward are not told.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and the Sages of his day
answer.event: The Sages sought to permit the Gibeonites to marry into the Jewish people.
answer.turn: Rabbi objected that even if they could waive the people's share in the Gibeonites, no one could waive the altar's share.
answer.outcome: Rabbi's objection blocked the proposal.
answer.summary: In the days of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, the Sages wanted to permit the Gibeonites to marry into the community. Rabbi stopped them: the court might give up the people's claim on the Gibeonites as servants, but who could give up the claim of the Temple altar?
answer.missing: The text does not state explicitly that the proposal was dropped.

answer.actor: Rav Mordekhai, reporting to Rav Ashi
answer.event: A bill of divorce lay closer to the woman than to the husband and was lost, and the husband later died.
answer.outcome: They required the woman to perform halitza, not relying on the divorce.
answer.summary: Rav Mordekhai told Rav Ashi of an actual case: a bill of divorce was thrown nearer to the wife than to the husband and was then lost. When the husband died, the authorities did not treat her as divorced and required her to perform halitza.
answer.missing: The details of the case are supplied only by the translator's gloss; the report itself is a bare one-line reference.

answer.actor: Rav Nahman and a woman from Mehoza married to a man from Neharde'a
answer.event: The couple came before Rav Nahman about her marriage contract, and he recognized her Mehoza accent and ruled by the custom of Babylonia, following Rav.
answer.turn: They told him she was marrying into Neharde'a.
answer.outcome: He reversed himself and ruled by Neharde'a's custom, following Shmuel.
answer.summary: A woman from Mehoza married a man from Neharde'a, and they came before Rav Nahman about her marriage contract. Hearing her accent, he ruled according to the custom of Babylonia. When they pointed out that she was marrying into Neharde'a, he changed his ruling to follow Neharde'a's custom instead.

answer.actor: A depositor, the late Hasa, and Rav Nahman
answer.event: A man deposited a silver goblet with Hasa, who died without leaving instructions about it.
answer.turn: Rav Nahman reasoned that Hasa was not wealthy enough to own such a goblet and that the claimant gave identifying marks.
answer.outcome: Rav Nahman ruled in favor of the depositor, provided he was not a frequent visitor to the house.
answer.summary: A man had left a silver goblet in Hasa's house, and Hasa died without saying anything about it. The case came to Rav Nahman, who said Hasa was known not to be rich and the claimant could describe the goblet, so the goblet went to the claimant, unless he was someone who regularly came and went there and could simply have seen it.

answer.actor: A man preparing a feast, and Rava
answer.event: A man prepared a betrothal feast on the ninetieth day after the woman's first husband died.
answer.turn: Rava prohibited it.
answer.outcome: The man lost his feast.
answer.summary: A man prepared a feast for his betrothal on the ninetieth day after his bride's first husband had died. Rava forbade it, and the man's feast went to waste. The Gemara adds that it was really a wedding feast, not a betrothal feast.

answer.event: Rav Hamnuna posed a challenge from a baraita, and Rava had no answer and fell silent.
answer.turn: After Rav Hamnuna left, Rava thought of an answer, doubted it, and then found a baraita confirming it.
answer.outcome: Rava concluded the challenge could be dismissed because the baraita follows Rabbi Elazar.
answer.summary: Rav Hamnuna challenged Rava with a baraita, and Rava stood silent. Once Rav Hamnuna had gone, Rava asked himself why he had not answered that the baraita follows Rabbi Elazar. He doubted his own answer, then recalled a teaching showing Rabbi Elazar held so even in this case, which settled it for him.
answer.missing: Rav Hamnuna's departure and the answer are never delivered to him; the encounter ends in Rava's own reflection.

answer.event: A case came before Rabbi about an alleyway closed on one side by the sea and on the other by a garbage dump.
answer.turn: Rabbi declined to rule.
answer.outcome: He said neither that carrying there was prohibited nor that it was permitted.
answer.summary: An alleyway ran from the sea at one end to a garbage dump at the other, and the question of whether one could carry in it on Shabbat was brought to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi. He gave no ruling at all, neither permitting nor forbidding it.

answer.event: Aher saw the tongue of the executed Hutzpit the disseminator being dragged along by a pig.
answer.turn: He cried out that a mouth that produced pearls should not lick the dust.
answer.outcome: He went out and sinned.
answer.summary: According to one tradition, Elisha ben Avuya saw the tongue of the martyred teacher Hutzpit being dragged through the dirt by a pig. Appalled, he asked how a mouth that had spoken pearls could end up licking dust, and from then on he abandoned the faith and sinned.

answer.actor: Unnamed people who weighed a turnip
answer.event: A fox nested inside a turnip, and people weighed it.
answer.turn: It turned out to weigh sixty litra even with the hollow.
answer.summary: As proof that produce can grow enormous, the Sages recalled a turnip so large that a fox made its den inside it. When people weighed it, it came to sixty litra by the measure of Tzippori.
answer.missing: It is cited only as a brief proof; there is no larger narrative or ending.

answer.actor: Rav Nahman, Rav Adda bar Ahava and Rav Hana
answer.event: Rav Nahman found Rav Adda bar Ahava and his son-in-law Rav Hana in the Pumbedita marketplace debating a mishna about a minor and a deaf-mute widow.
answer.turn: Rav Nahman told them their distinction did not hold.
answer.summary: Rav Nahman came upon Rav Adda bar Ahava and his son-in-law Rav Hana in the Pumbedita marketplace, trading arguments about when levirate marriage with one widow frees her co-wife. They proposed that if the dead brother was deaf-mute the question resolves itself; Rav Nahman told them it remains uncertain even then.
answer.missing: The encounter is a frame for a legal argument; their reaction to Rav Nahman is not given.

answer.actor: Ravina and Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak
answer.event: Ravina found Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak leaning on a door bar, pondering a legal question.
answer.outcome: The question was left unresolved.
answer.summary: Ravina came upon Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak leaning on the bar of a door, lost in thought over whether a husband who says only "void" about a bill of divorce has cancelled it. No answer was found.
answer.missing: There is a scene but no turn; it frames an unresolved legal question.

answer.actor: Rav Yosef and two claimants holding deeds
answer.event: Two deeds to the same property came before Rav Yosef, one dated the fifth of Nisan and one dated only Nisan, and he awarded the property to the fifth-of-Nisan holder.
answer.turn: The losing claimant protested and then asked for a writ to repossess property sold from Iyyar onward.
answer.outcome: Rav Yosef refused, since buyers could claim his deed dated from the first of Nisan.
answer.summary: Two men brought deeds for the same property to Rav Yosef: one dated the fifth of Nisan, the other simply Nisan. Rav Yosef gave the property to the man with the exact date. When the other protested, he was told his deed could be from late in the month; when he then asked for a writ to collect from buyers after Iyyar, Rav Yosef said those buyers could argue his deed was from the first of Nisan, so he should claim the field itself.

answer.actor: Rabba bar Avuh and Rav Nahman
answer.event: Rabba bar Avuh told the Sages to examine Rav Nahman in the bathhouse, promising his daughter if his body gave off steam.
answer.summary: Rabba bar Avuh, considering Rav Nahman as a husband for his daughter, told the Sages to watch him while bathing: if his flesh gave off steam, a sign of virility, he would give him his daughter.
answer.missing: The result of the examination and whether the marriage happened.

answer.actor: A man who fell into the Great Cistern; Rabbi Meir
answer.event: A man fell into the Great Cistern and came out after three days.
answer.summary: Rabbi Meir cited a case of a man who fell into the Great Cistern and came out alive three days later. The Sages objected that miracles are not used to decide law.
answer.missing: The incident is only referenced by its opening words from the mishna; its full account is not in the segments shown.

answer.actor: A man who betrothed a woman too early, and Rafram
answer.event: A man betrothed a woman within three months of her divorce or widowhood and then fled.
answer.outcome: Rafram ruled that his flight was punishment enough and he was not excommunicated.
answer.summary: A man betrothed a woman during the three months she was required to wait, and then fled. When the case was brought to Rafram, he ruled that running away was enough of a penalty and no excommunication was needed.
answer.missing: The incident is reported only as a bare case serving a legal dispute.

answer.event: While Rabbi Elazar sat absorbed in Torah study in Tzippori's lower market, his cloak lay forgotten in the upper market, and a man came to take it.
answer.turn: The would-be thief found a serpent lying on the cloak.
answer.outcome: The cloak was protected; the man could not take it.
answer.summary: Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat was so absorbed in Torah study that he would sit studying in the lower marketplace of Tzippori while his cloak lay in the upper marketplace. Once a man came to steal the cloak, but found a serpent lying on it, guarding it.

answer.actor: Pishon the camel driver and his wife
answer.event: The wife of Pishon the camel driver refused (annulled) her marriage to him in his absence.
answer.turn: Pishon had mismanaged her property, so the Sages dealt with him by a 'defective measure' in return.
answer.outcome: Her refusal in his absence was allowed to stand as a punishment to him.
answer.summary: Pishon the camel driver mishandled the property his wife brought into the marriage. When she declared her refusal to remain married to him, it was done in his absence, and the Sages let it stand, measuring him with the same defective measure he had used.
answer.missing: The events themselves are only cited in a legal debate; what Pishon actually did and how the annulment proceeded are not narrated.

answer.event: Rabbi Shabbtai's widowed daughter-in-law seized a saddlebag full of coins for her sustenance.
answer.turn: The Sages tried to take it back from her.
answer.outcome: The Sages had no power to remove it from her possession.
answer.summary: Rav Dimi reported that Rabbi Shabbtai's daughter-in-law grabbed a saddlebag full of coins to support herself. The Sages found they had no authority to take it back from her, and she kept it.

answer.event: Rav arrived at Damharya and issued a practical ruling about a breach in a wall.
answer.turn: Rav Hanan bar Rava claimed Rav had only done so because he found an unguarded valley and fenced it in.
answer.summary: Rav once came to a place called Damharya and issued a practical ruling there, which Rav Huna cited as support for his view. Rav Hanan bar Rava answered that Rav had acted only because he found an unguarded valley and fenced it in as a special precaution.
answer.missing: The incident is only cited as precedent in a legal dispute; what Rav saw and did at Damharya is not told.

answer.event: The Rabbis urged Rav Sheshet to marry and have sons, and he answered that his daughter's sons are his sons.
answer.turn: His answer was a deflection; the real reason was that he had become impotent from waiting through Rav Huna's long lectures.
answer.outcome: He did not remarry.
answer.summary: The Rabbis told Rav Sheshet to marry and father sons. He replied that his daughter's sons counted as his own. The Gemara explains he was only putting them off: he had become impotent from sitting through Rav Huna's lengthy discourses.
answer.missing: The outcome (that he did not remarry) is implied, not stated.

answer.event: Rav Hinnana bar Shelamiya was teaching a mishna to Hiyya bar Rav in Rav's presence.
answer.turn: Rav rebuked him for teaching it according to the lone opinion of Rabbi Meir rather than the Rabbis.
answer.summary: Rav Hinnana bar Shelamiya was teaching Rav's son Hiyya a mishna in front of Rav, formulating it in a stringent way. Rav challenged him: had he abandoned the majority of the Rabbis to follow Rabbi Meir?
answer.missing: No response or outcome to Rav's rebuke is given; the rest is legal explanation.

answer.actor: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
answer.event: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba met Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi hurrying his grandson to the synagogue with only a cheap cloth on his head.
answer.turn: Asked why such haste, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi cited the verse equating teaching one's grandchildren with standing at Sinai.
answer.outcome: From then on Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba would not eat breakfast until he had reviewed and added to his child's studies.
answer.summary: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba saw Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rushing his grandchild to study, a cheap covering thrown on his head. When he asked why such a fuss, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi quoted the verse linking teaching one's grandchildren to standing at Sinai. Moved, Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba resolved never to eat breakfast before teaching his child; Rabba bar Rav Huna likewise would not eat before bringing his child to the study hall.

answer.actor: A depositor and the estate of Rav Dimi
answer.event: A man deposited silk with Rav Dimi, who died without leaving instructions about it.
answer.turn: The ownership was disputed before Rabbi Abba, who knew Rav Dimi was not wealthy and noted the claimant gave an identifying mark.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Abba awarded the silk to the claimant.
answer.summary: A man left silk in the house of Rav Dimi, Rav Safra's brother, and Rav Dimi died without saying anything about it. The case came before Rabbi Abba, who ruled the silk belonged to the claimant, since Rav Dimi was known to be poor and the claimant could describe a distinguishing mark.

answer.event: Reish Lakish demanded proof of priestly status from teruma, and Rabbi Elazar objected that priesthood does not vanish where there is no threshing floor.
answer.turn: Later, when the same case came before Rabbi Yohanan, Rabbi Yohanan made the very same objection, revealing that Rabbi Elazar had been quoting him.
answer.outcome: Reish Lakish glared at Rabbi Elazar and rebuked him for not citing Rabbi Yohanan by name.
answer.summary: A man testified before Reish Lakish that someone was a priest because he read first from the Torah. Reish Lakish demanded to know if he had seen him receive teruma, and Rabbi Elazar objected. Later, before Rabbi Yohanan, the same thing happened and Rabbi Yohanan gave Rabbi Elazar's exact objection. Reish Lakish glared at Rabbi Elazar: you heard this from the blacksmith's son and didn't tell us it was his?

answer.event: A son-in-law passed by the door of his father-in-law's house.
answer.turn: There were rumors about him and his mother-in-law.
answer.outcome: Rav Sheshet had him flogged.
answer.summary: A certain man walked past the entrance of his father-in-law's house, and Rav Sheshet had him flogged. The reason was that there were already rumors of an affair between him and his mother-in-law, and his passing by fed them.
answer.missing: The case is cited briefly within a legal discussion; little of the incident itself is told.

answer.event: Rav Malkiyyu arranged a marriage for a deaf-mute neighbor and wrote the bride a 400-dinar marriage contract from the man's property.
answer.turn: Though the deaf-mute was not obligated to give a marriage contract, Rav Malkiyyu reasoned that a wife served him even better than a maidservant whom the court would buy him.
answer.outcome: Rava praised Rav Malkiyyu's wisdom.
answer.summary: A deaf-mute man lived near Rav Malkiyyu, who married him off and wrote the wife a 400-dinar marriage contract from his property. Rav Malkiyyu reasoned that if the court would buy him a maidservant, all the more so a wife. Rava admired him: who is as wise as Rav Malkiyyu?

answer.event: In a shepherds' village an alleyway ending in a backyard was brought before Rav Yehuda for a ruling.
answer.outcome: He required nothing further to permit carrying there.
answer.summary: Rav Yosef recalled a case in a shepherds' village where an alleyway ended in a backyard. The matter came before Rav Yehuda, who ruled that nothing was needed to permit carrying in it.
answer.missing: Only a bare report of a ruling; no development or turn in the incident.

answer.actor: The widow of Rav Yosef son of Rav Menashya
answer.event: A widow came before Rav Yosef demanding sustenance, then wine, then silk garments.
answer.turn: When Rav Yosef asked why she needed silk, she retorted it was for him and his colleagues, so she would not be shamed before them.
answer.outcome: Her retort stands as the final word.
answer.summary: The widow of Rav Yosef son of Rav Menashya of D'vil came to Rav Yosef for support. He granted her food, then wine. When she asked for silk clothes and he asked why, she answered: for you, your friends and your friends' friends, so that she need not be ashamed before the scholars.
answer.missing: It is not stated whether Rav Yosef granted the silk.

answer.event: While Rabbi Yehuda and others sat before Rabbi Tarfon, a yevama came to perform halitza.
answer.turn: Rabbi Tarfon instructed all present to call out 'He who had his shoe removed' three times.
answer.summary: Rabbi Yehuda recalled sitting before Rabbi Tarfon when a widow came to perform the halitza ceremony. Rabbi Tarfon told everyone present to answer together, three times, 'He who had his shoe removed.'
answer.missing: The ceremony's conclusion is not told; the incident is a brief precedent.

answer.event: Rav Kahana asked Rav Ashi to testify for him, prompting his memory, but Rav Ashi said he did not remember.
answer.turn: Rav Ashi eventually remembered and testified, but Rav Kahana hesitated, fearing he had influenced the testimony.
answer.outcome: Rav Ashi assured him he had recalled it through his own effort, not by relying on Rav Kahana.
answer.summary: Rav Kahana needed Rav Ashi's testimony and tried to jog his memory, but Rav Ashi insisted he did not remember. Later Rav Ashi recalled the matter and testified. Seeing Rav Kahana uneasy that he had planted the memory, Rav Ashi told him: do you think I am relying on you? I worked at it and remembered on my own.

answer.actor: Rabbi Shimon bar Abba, Rabbi Elai and Rabbi Ya'akov bar Zavdi
answer.event: Rabbi Elai and Rabbi Ya'akov bar Zavdi were studying when Rabbi Shimon bar Abba passed by, and they stood for him.
answer.turn: Rabbi Shimon bar Abba objected that they were ordained and he was not, and that Torah does not stand before its students.
answer.outcome: He told them they need not have stood.
answer.summary: Two scholars, Rabbi Elai and Rabbi Ya'akov bar Zavdi, were sitting and studying when Rabbi Shimon bar Abba walked by, and they rose for him. He told them they should not have: they were ordained and he was merely an associate, and besides, the Torah they were studying does not stand up for those who study it.

answer.actor: Bonyam ben Nunyam and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
answer.event: A wealthy man, Bonyam ben Nunyam, sent Rabbi a gift of four kinds of extremely fine linen.
answer.summary: A wealthy man named Bonyam ben Nunyam once sent Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi a gift of four special linens, so fine they could be folded to the size of a nut or a pistachio. The passage then uses the gift to explain a word.
answer.missing: Any turn or outcome; the report is a single event used to gloss a word.

answer.actor: A man who betrothed a woman; Rav Shimi bar Hiyya
answer.event: A man betrothed a woman with a bundle of rags, and Rav Shimi bar Hiyya, sitting before Rav, examined it to see if it was worth a peruta.
answer.summary: A man betrothed a woman using a bundle of rags. Rav Shimi bar Hiyya, sitting before Rav, examined the bundle to determine whether it was worth a peruta, since only then would the betrothal be valid.
answer.missing: The result of the examination: whether the rags were worth a peruta and whether she was betrothed.

answer.event: When Rav Nahman came to Neharde'a he ordered the earth cleared away from the alleyway doors.
answer.summary: When Rav Nahman came to Neharde'a, he told people to clear away the earth that blocked the alleyway doors so they could be closed. The rest is legal analysis of why he gave this instruction.
answer.missing: Whether the order was carried out and what followed; the passage turns at once to legal inference.

answer.event: A man asked Rabbi Yosei whether a widow could perform halitza within three months of her husband's death.
answer.turn: Rabbi Yosei refused, and when the man pressed him on what harm it would do, Rabbi Yosei answered with a verse.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Yosei justified his ruling from Deuteronomy 25:7: only one eligible for levirate marriage is eligible for halitza.
answer.summary: A man came to Rabbi Yosei and asked whether halitza could be done within three months of the husband's death. Rabbi Yosei said no. The man pushed back, asking what the harm would be, and Rabbi Yosei answered by citing a verse, teaching that only a woman eligible for levirate marriage may perform halitza.

answer.actor: Abaye, Rav Safra and Rav Yosef
answer.event: Abaye was teaching Rav Yosef's ruling when Rav Safra challenged him with two objections from mishnayot.
answer.turn: Abaye answered the first objection but fell silent at the second.
answer.outcome: Abaye reported the exchange to Rav Yosef, who told him the answer he should have given: members of a Paschal group are vigilant.
answer.summary: Abaye sat teaching a ruling in Rav Yosef's name, and Rav Safra raised an objection from a mishna. Abaye rebutted it, but Rav Safra raised a second objection about lowering the Paschal lamb into the oven, and Abaye had no reply. When Abaye later told Rav Yosef what had happened, Rav Yosef asked why he had not answered that members of a Paschal group are vigilant.

answer.actor: Levi, Ze'eiri and Rav Shimi bar Hiyya
answer.event: Straw, fodder and water were brought to these three sages through human partitions on Shabbat.
answer.summary: On Shabbat, straw was brought in for Levi, fodder for Ze'eiri, and water for Rav Shimi bar Hiyya, carried through partitions formed by people who did not know they were being used that way.
answer.missing: Any turn or outcome; it is a terse list of precedents.

answer.actor: Rava, a yavam and yevama, and Rav Sherevya
answer.event: A couple who admitted they had not consummated their levirate marriage came before Rava, who ordered halitza for her.
answer.turn: Rav Sherevya objected that a baraita requires both a bill of divorce and halitza.
answer.outcome: Rava retracted: if the baraita is taught, it is taught.
answer.summary: A yavam and yevama who both admitted they had never consummated their levirate marriage came before Rava. He told the sages to arrange halitza and settle her case. Rav Sherevya objected that a baraita requires a divorce as well as halitza, and Rava accepted the correction and withdrew his ruling.

answer.event: After his interlocutor proposed that Rabbi Yohanan meant the ascents and descents of Eretz Yisrael, Rav Dimi praised him.
answer.turn: Rav Dimi recognized that the questioner had grasped Rabbi Yohanan's meaning as if he had been there.
answer.summary: In a legal exchange, a scholar guessed that Rabbi Yohanan's ruling referred to the hills and slopes of Eretz Yisrael. Rav Dimi, who had heard Rabbi Yohanan, praised him: it was as if he had seen the man's head among the pillars of the study hall when Rabbi Yohanan taught it.
answer.missing: The exchange is mostly legal argument; the only event is the compliment.

answer.event: Rav Yosef said he had never heard a certain ruling of Rav.
answer.turn: Abaye reminded him that he himself had taught it to them, and recounted the occasion.
answer.summary: Rav Yosef said he had never heard a certain teaching. His student Abaye told him that he himself had taught it to them, and reminded him of the exact discussion about brothers eating at their father's table, where he had quoted Rav.
answer.missing: Rav Yosef's response; also the reason he had forgotten (illness) is supplied only by the translation.

answer.event: A woman, mourning her husband, removed him from his grave.
answer.summary: The Rabbis point to an incident in which a certain woman removed her husband from his grave, as proof that temptation can overcome a person even in mourning. The text itself only alludes to the incident.
answer.missing: The story itself: the Hebrew only alludes to it; the details (the guard, the stolen body, the affair) come from the translator's gloss.

answer.actor: A debtor, his creditor, and the purchaser of his land
answer.event: A man owing 100 dinars sold two plots for 50 each; his creditor seized one plot and then came for the other.
answer.turn: The purchaser went to the creditor with 100 dinars and offered either the one plot as full payment or the cash in exchange for giving up claims on both.
answer.summary: A man who owed 100 dinars sold his two small fields to a buyer for 50 each. The creditor seized one field and then came to take the other. The buyer brought him 100 dinars and said: either take this field as worth 100, or take the money and give up your claim to both.
answer.missing: The creditor's answer or the court's ruling; what follows is legal discussion.

answer.actor: Rabba bar bar Hanna and an Arab
answer.event: Rabba bar bar Hanna saw an Arab cut open his camel with a sword.
answer.turn: The camel died so quickly it did not even stop braying.
answer.outcome: The camel was dead at once.
answer.summary: Rabba bar bar Hanna reported seeing an Arab slash open his camel with a sword. The camel died so fast that it never finished its bray. The Gemara cites this as evidence, and Abaye answers that the camel must have been weak.

answer.event: A heretic taunted Rabban Gamliel that God had removed Himself from Israel, citing Hoshea 5:6.
answer.turn: Rabban Gamliel pointed out that the verse says 'from them', meaning Israel removed itself from God.
answer.outcome: Rabban Gamliel called him a fool and concluded that such a removal has no force, like a halitza done by the brothers.
answer.summary: A heretic mocked Rabban Gamliel, saying the Jews are a people whose God has done halitza with them, citing a verse in Hosea. Rabban Gamliel called him a fool: the verse says 'from them', not 'to them', so it is Israel who withdrew from God. And a halitza done by the brothers to the widow means nothing, so the bond remains.

answer.actor: The Israelites and the young women of Jabesh-gilead
answer.event: The Israelites found four hundred virgins among the people of Jabesh-gilead, and Rav Kahana explains how they told virgins from non-virgins.
answer.summary: Scripture says four hundred virgins were found at Jabesh-gilead. Rav Kahana explains that they were sat on the opening of a wine barrel: a non-virgin's breath would smell of wine and a virgin's would not.
answer.missing: The passage is an exegetical explanation of a biblical event, not a narrated episode with a turn and ending.

answer.event: A father told his son to climb a building and bring him chicks; the son sent away the mother bird and took the young.
answer.turn: Though he was fulfilling two mitzvot promising long life, he fell on the way down.
answer.outcome: He died, which Rabbi Ya'akov takes as proof that the promised reward is in the World to Come.
answer.summary: A father asked his son to climb up and bring him some chicks. The son climbed up, sent away the mother bird and took the young, keeping both the mitzva of honoring his father and of sending away the mother bird, each of which promises long life. On the way down he fell and died. Rabbi Ya'akov concludes that the reward must refer to the World to Come.

answer.actor: Mar Yehuda and Rav Huna bar Yehuda
answer.event: Mar Yehuda visited Rav Huna bar Yehuda and saw people carrying among trees not planted in rows.
answer.turn: He challenged Rav Huna for not following Avimi's ruling.
answer.outcome: Rav Huna replied that he follows Rav Nahman's opinion.
answer.summary: Mar Yehuda visited Rav Huna bar Yehuda's house and saw people carrying on Shabbat among trees that were not planted in rows. He asked whether Rav Huna did not follow Avimi's ruling, and Rav Huna explained that he followed Rav Nahman, who permits it.

answer.actor: An Amorite and a resident of Eretz Yisrael
answer.event: An Amorite asked a resident of Eretz Yisrael how much fruit they picked from a palm tree by the Jordan.
answer.turn: When told sixty kor, the Amorite scoffed that they had ruined the land, since his people got 120.
answer.outcome: The resident answered that he had only counted one side of the tree.
answer.summary: An Amorite asked a man of Eretz Yisrael how many dates they picked from a certain palm on the Jordan's bank. The man said sixty kor. The Amorite mocked him, saying they had ruined the land already, since his people used to pick 120. The man replied that he had been talking about only one side of the tree.

answer.actor: A man who betrothed a minor girl; Ravina
answer.event: A man betrothed a minor girl with a bundle of vegetables in the marketplace without her father's consent.
answer.outcome: Ravina ruled that a degrading betrothal raises no concern that the father approved.
answer.summary: A man betrothed a minor girl in the marketplace using a bundle of vegetables, without her father's consent. Ravina ruled that even those who worry the father might have approved would not worry here, because the betrothal was done in a degrading way.
answer.missing: The case ends in a legal ruling rather than in an outcome for the people involved.

answer.event: A case came before Rabbi Yitzhak in Antioch, and he ruled that collecting in the debtor's absence with an oath applies only to a marriage contract.
answer.summary: Rav Aha Sar HaBira reported that a case came before Rabbi Yitzhak in Antioch, and Rabbi Yitzhak ruled that a woman may collect her marriage contract in her husband's absence with an oath, but a creditor may not.
answer.missing: The incident itself: who was involved and what happened is not told, only the ruling.

answer.actor: The daughter-in-law of Nakdimon ben Guryon
answer.event: The Sages allotted the widowed daughter-in-law of Nakdimon ben Guryon two se'a of wine a week for cooking, and she blessed them that they should allot the same to their own daughters.
answer.turn: She was a widow waiting for her yavam, so her blessing implied wishing her plight on their daughters.
answer.outcome: The Sages did not answer amen to her blessing.
answer.summary: After her husband died, the Sages granted the daughter-in-law of the wealthy Nakdimon ben Guryon two se'a of wine every week for her cooking. Grateful, she blessed them: may you allot the same to your daughters. But she was a widow bound to her brother-in-law, so the Sages refused to answer amen, not wanting their daughters to end up in her situation.

answer.actor: The sister of Rami bar Hama and her husband Rav Avya
answer.event: The marriage contract of Rami bar Hama's sister, wife of Rav Avya, was lost and the couple came before Rav Yosef.
answer.turn: Rav Yosef cited Shmuel that the ruling forbidding a couple without a full marriage contract is only Rabbi Meir's view.
answer.summary: Rami bar Hama's sister was married to Rav Avya. Her marriage contract was lost, and the couple went to Rav Yosef to ask what to do. He told them that the view that such a couple may not live together belongs to Rabbi Meir.
answer.missing: The passage itself is only the introductory line; the problem comes in the next segment, and the final ruling for the couple is not shown.

answer.event: Walking on the road with a woman ahead of them, Rav urged Rav Yehuda to hurry away from her.
answer.turn: Rav Yehuda objected that Rav himself permitted it for men of fit morals, and Rav answered that he did not mean men like themselves.
answer.outcome: Rav clarified he meant only men like Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi and his colleagues.
answer.summary: Rav and his student Rav Yehuda were travelling when a woman was walking ahead of them. Rav told him to speed up and escape 'Gehenna' rather than be secluded with her. Rav Yehuda reminded him that he had ruled it permitted for upright men; Rav answered that he did not mean the likes of the two of them, but only proven saints such as Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi and his colleagues.

answer.actor: A man who betrothed a woman with stolen coins
answer.event: A man snatched coins from someone and threw them to a woman washing her feet, declaring her betrothed to him.
answer.turn: The case came before Rava, who held that the owner of stolen money is not presumed to have given up on it.
answer.outcome: Rava ruled the betrothal ineffective.
answer.summary: A woman was washing her feet in a basin when a man grabbed some coins from another person, threw them to her, and said 'You are betrothed to me.' The matter came before Rava, who ruled that no one follows Rabbi Shimon's view that a robbery victim gives up on his money; the coins were not the man's, so the betrothal did not take effect.

answer.event: A man let witnesses trace their names on ordinary financial documents.
answer.turn: That leniency applied only to bills of divorce.
answer.outcome: Rav Kahana had him flogged.
answer.summary: Someone applied the leniency of letting illiterate witnesses trace their signatures to ordinary financial documents, not just bills of divorce. Rav Kahana had him flogged for it.
answer.missing: It is a one-line report; who the person was and the circumstances are not given.

answer.actor: A man who came before Rabban Gamliel
answer.event: A man complained to Rabban Gamliel that he found his bride without signs of virginity.
answer.turn: Rabban Gamliel suggested he had diverted his approach, illustrating with a parable of a door found open or locked.
answer.summary: A man came to Rabban Gamliel claiming he had found his bride's opening unobstructed. Rabban Gamliel suggested that perhaps he had come at it at an angle (or, in another version, forced it), and compared him to a man in the dark who finds a door open or locked depending on whether he moves the bolt.
answer.missing: How the case was resolved is not stated.

answer.actor: A herdsman for orphans and a creditor
answer.event: A creditor seized an ox from a herdsman caring for orphans' cattle, and they disputed whether he seized it before or after the debtor's death.
answer.turn: Rav Nahman asked whether there were witnesses to the seizure, and there were none.
answer.outcome: Rav Nahman ruled for the creditor, since he could have claimed he bought it, he is believed that he seized it during the debtor's lifetime.
answer.summary: A creditor took an ox from the herdsman who looked after some orphans' cattle, to pay their late father's debt. The creditor said he took it while the father was alive; the herdsman said it was after his death. Rav Nahman asked the herdsman whether anyone saw the seizure; no one had, so he ruled that the creditor, who could have claimed to have bought the ox, is believed.

answer.event: During a famine in Rav Yosef's time, the Sages asked him to pray for mercy.
answer.turn: He refused, pointing out that even Elisha, who supported 2,200 scholars, did not pray in a time of divine anger.
answer.summary: In Rav Yosef's day there was a famine seen as divine anger, and the Sages asked him to pray. He declined, arguing that if Elisha, who fed 2,200 scholars, did not pray at such a time, he should not either.
answer.missing: What happened after his refusal is not shown.

answer.event: Rabbi Hanina sent his weekly four dinars for a poor man via his wife.
answer.turn: She overheard the household asking whether he dined on silver or gold tablecloths and concluded he did not need charity.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Hanina responded by citing Rabbi Elazar that we should be grateful to swindlers, since they excuse our failings toward the truly poor.
answer.summary: Rabbi Hanina used to send four dinars to a certain poor man every Friday. One week he sent his wife, who came back saying the man did not need it: she had overheard his family asking whether he would dine on the silver or the gold tablecloths. Rabbi Hanina remarked, quoting Rabbi Elazar, that we should appreciate swindlers, because without them we would be guilty every day of neglecting the real poor.

answer.actor: A betrothed couple before Rav Yosef
answer.event: A pregnant betrothed woman and her fiance came before Rav Yosef; she said the child was his.
answer.turn: He confirmed that it was his.
answer.outcome: Rav Yosef ruled there was no concern, since the man admitted paternity and in any case the halakha follows Rabban Gamliel.
answer.summary: A betrothed woman became pregnant before the wedding, and she and her fiance came to Rav Yosef. She said she had conceived from him, and he agreed. Rav Yosef ruled there was nothing to worry about: the man admitted it, and the law trusts her claim anyway.

answer.event: Ravina, holding his orphaned nephew's wine, was taking his own wine to Sikhra to sell.
answer.turn: He asked Rav Ashi whether he could take the orphan's wine along.
answer.outcome: Rav Ashi told him to go, since the orphan's wine needs no better treatment than his own.
answer.summary: Ravina was looking after wine belonging to his orphaned nephew, Ravina the younger, and was taking his own wine to Sikhra to sell. He asked Rav Ashi whether he could bring the orphan's wine too. Rav Ashi told him to go ahead: the orphan's wine deserved no better than his own.

answer.event: Shimon ben Azzai found a lineage scroll in Jerusalem.
answer.turn: It recorded that a certain man was a mamzer, that Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov's teachings were few but sound, and that Manasseh killed Isaiah.
answer.summary: Shimon ben Azzai reported finding a genealogical scroll in Jerusalem. It recorded that a certain person was a mamzer, praised Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov's teachings as small but clean, and stated that King Manasseh killed the prophet Isaiah.
answer.missing: It is a report of a find and its contents; nothing follows from the discovery within the passage.

answer.event: A marriage contract with a recognized scribal formula and one verified witness signature came before Rabbi Abbahu.
answer.turn: Rabbi Abbahu intended to validate it, but Rabbi Yirmeya objected that the scribe must have signed, not merely written it.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Yirmeya's correction stood against validating it.
answer.summary: A marriage contract was brought to Rabbi Abbahu; people recognized the scribe's handwriting and one witness's signature. Rabbi Abbahu was inclined to accept it on that basis. Rabbi Yirmeya stopped him: the law speaks of a scribe who signed, and his handwriting alone is not enough.
answer.missing: Whether Rabbi Abbahu then rejected the document is implied, not stated.

answer.event: Rav Kahana, a priest, took a cloth as redemption for a firstborn son and declared that to him it was worth five sela.
answer.outcome: The redemption was accepted on his valuation.
answer.summary: When a man had to redeem his firstborn son, Rav Kahana, a priest, took a cloth from his house instead of five silver coins, saying that to him the cloth was worth five sela.
answer.missing: It is cited as a brief precedent; the second report (Mar bar Rav Ashi buying a cloth) is a separate one-line illustration.

answer.event: On his deathbed Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi summoned his younger son Rabbi Shimon and passed him the orders of wisdom, then his older son Rabban Gamliel and passed him the procedures of the patriarchate.
answer.turn: He divided his legacy, and instructed Rabban Gamliel to rule assertively and instill fear in the students.
answer.summary: As he was dying, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi asked for his younger son, Rabbi Shimon, and handed him the teachings of wisdom. Then he asked for his elder son, Rabban Gamliel, gave him the procedures of the office of Nasi, and told him to lead with a firm hand and keep the students in awe.
answer.missing: The beginning of the deathbed narrative and its end (his death) lie outside the segments shown.

answer.actor: A man who came before Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
answer.event: A man testified to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that someone was a Levite because he was called second to the Torah.
answer.turn: Asked whether that might reflect prominence rather than lineage, he answered that a priest had read before him.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi granted the man Levite status on that testimony.
answer.summary: A man told Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that he had seen someone established as a Levite, because he was called second to the Torah in synagogue. The rabbi asked whether he was called as a Levite or merely as an important man; the witness replied that a priest had read just before him. On that basis Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi recognized the man as a Levite.

answer.event: The Sages asked Rabbi Abbahu, in riddling language, where Rabbi Elai was hiding.
answer.turn: He answered in a riddle that Elai had taken a lively young wife of priestly family who had kept him awake.
answer.summary: The Sages, speaking in wordplay, asked Rabbi Abbahu where Rabbi Elai had disappeared to. He answered in a riddle of his own: Elai had married a lively young woman of priestly descent, his second wife, and she had kept him up all night.
answer.missing: It is a single exchange of wit; nothing further happens.

answer.actor: Anan bar Hiyya of Hagra / the Sages investigating a found bill of divorce
answer.event: A bill of divorce was found in Sura in the name of Anan bar Hiyya of Neharde'a, and the Sages searched the whole region and found only one man of that name.
answer.turn: Witnesses testified that on the day the document was written, that Anan bar Hiyya was with them in Neharde'a, not in Sura.
answer.outcome: The case ends in a legal disagreement: Abaye says there is no concern, Rava says he might have travelled miraculously fast or given instructions remotely; no ruling on the woman is narrated.
answer.summary: A divorce document was found in Sura, signed in the name of Anan bar Hiyya of Neharde'a. The Sages searched from Sura to Neharde'a and found only one man by that name, Anan bar Hiyya of Hagra. But witnesses came and said that on the day the document was written he had been with them in Neharde'a. Abaye and Rava then argued over whether the document could still be his.
answer.missing: What actually happened to the document and the woman; the passage turns into a legal debate rather than an ending.

answer.actor: A debtor who hid his money behind a gentile
answer.event: A debtor claimed his money belonged to a gentile so his creditor could not collect it.
answer.turn: Because he acted improperly, the Sages acted improperly with him.
answer.outcome: The Sages forced him to sell his land himself and pay the creditor.
answer.summary: Rav Pappa asked Rav Hama about a ruling attributed to Rava, that a debtor can be made to sell his land himself to pay a creditor. Rav Hama explained the real incident behind it: the debtor had pretended his money belonged to a gentile to avoid paying. Because he behaved dishonestly, the Sages dealt harshly with him and made him sell the land.
answer.missing: The incident is only summarized in a sentence; no details of who, when, or how it was carried out.

answer.actor: The son of Nehunya the well digger
answer.event: Despite his father's merit in digging wells for the public, Nehunya's son died of thirst.
answer.turn: His father's merit did not protect him, which Rabbi Abba explains as God being exacting to a hair's breadth with the righteous.
answer.outcome: The son died.
answer.summary: Nehunya dug wells for travellers, and when his daughter fell into a cistern she was saved, as Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa had foreseen. Yet Rabbi Abba reports that even so Nehunya's son died of thirst. He explains this with verses teaching that God is extremely exacting with those closest to Him.
answer.missing: The story of the son's death itself is only stated, not narrated; how or why he died is not told.

answer.event: An uncircumcised priest sprinkled the purification waters.
