answer.outcome: The Sages ruled his sprinkling valid.
answer.summary: A baraita reports an incident in which an uncircumcised man sprinkled the waters of purification, and the Sages declared his sprinkling valid.
answer.missing: Who the man was, why he was uncircumcised, and any circumstances; the incident is a one-line precedent.

answer.event: Funerals had become so expensive that families abandoned their dead and fled.
answer.turn: Rabban Gamliel instructed that he himself be buried in plain linen.
answer.outcome: Everyone followed his example, and the custom of simple burial garments took hold, down to Rav Pappa's day.
answer.summary: Funerals once cost so much that relatives found the burial harder than the death and would sometimes leave the body and run away. Rabban Gamliel set an example by asking to be buried in simple linen. Everyone followed him, and by Rav Pappa's time people were buried even in cheap rough cloth.

answer.actor: A man captured with his mother
answer.event: A man, speaking casually, said that when he and his mother were held captive among gentiles he never stopped watching over her.
answer.turn: Though a son cannot normally testify for his mother, his remark was an unconsidered aside.
answer.outcome: Rabbi permitted the mother to marry a priest on the strength of his words.
answer.summary: A man chatting offhandedly mentioned that he and his mother had been taken captive, and that whether he went to draw water or gather wood, his mind was always on her. The case came before Rabbi (or Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi). Because the remark was casual and not formal testimony, Rabbi relied on it and allowed the mother to marry a priest.

answer.event: Rav Kahana held beer belonging to the orphan Rav Mesharshiyya bar Hilkai and put off selling it until the Festival.
answer.turn: He reasoned that even if it soured slightly, it would fetch ready cash at the Festival.
answer.summary: Rav Kahana was looking after beer owned by an orphan, Rav Mesharshiyya bar Hilkai. Instead of selling it at once, he waited for the Festival, explaining that even if it spoiled a bit, it would sell then for good cash.
answer.missing: Whether the plan worked or how the sale turned out.

answer.actor: Residents of a crooked alleyway in Sura
answer.event: Residents of an L-shaped alleyway in Sura set a rolled-up mat at its bend as a side post so they could carry on Shabbat.
answer.turn: Rav Hisda said the arrangement matched neither Rav nor Shmuel.
answer.outcome: The mat was declared ineffective, since the wind could blow it over.
answer.summary: In Sura there was an L-shaped alleyway where people placed a rolled mat at the corner to allow carrying on Shabbat. Rav Hisda ruled it worthless under either Rav's or Shmuel's view, because a loose mat that the wind can knock down is not a real side post.
answer.missing: Little action beyond the ruling; what the residents did afterward is not told.

answer.actor: Rav Pappa and Yehuda bar Mareimar
answer.event: Rav Pappa went to write the marriage contract for his son's bride, and Yehuda bar Mareimar came out to honor him.
answer.turn: At the door of the bride's house Yehuda tried to take his leave, and Rav Pappa saw he was unwilling to enter and asked why.
answer.summary: Rav Pappa arranged for his son to marry into the family of Abba of Sura and went to oversee the writing of the marriage contract. Yehuda bar Mareimar came out to greet him, but at the door he tried to leave. Rav Pappa invited him in and, seeing his reluctance, asked whether it was because of Shmuel's teaching against taking part in transferring an inheritance.
answer.missing: Yehuda's answer and whether he went in; the ending lies beyond the segments shown.

answer.actor: The Sages, Rav, and the messengers
answer.event: Faced with the Shmuel-Karna dispute about a minor betrothed without her father's consent, the Sages sent the question to Rav with the names of the two opinions swapped.
answer.turn: Rav, thinking Shmuel held the opposite view, swore by God that she needs both a bill of divorce and refusal.
answer.outcome: Rav declared that Shmuel would never say otherwise, unknowingly endorsing Shmuel's real opinion.
answer.summary: Shmuel ruled that a minor betrothed without her father's consent needs both a divorce and refusal, and Karna found this contradictory. The Sages sent the question to Rav but reversed whose opinion was whose. Rav swore that she needs both, and said heaven forbid Shmuel should say anything else, thereby backing Shmuel without knowing it.
answer.missing: Why the names were reversed and how Rav's answer was received.

answer.actor: A man who made a conditional divorce
answer.event: A man gave a bill of divorce that would take effect if he did not return within thirty days.
answer.turn: He came back just in time but the ferry was on the far side, so he stood at the river shouting 'See that I came!'
answer.outcome: Shmuel ruled that this did not count as returning, so the divorce took effect.
answer.summary: A man handed over a bill of divorce on condition that it would be valid if he did not come back within thirty days. At the end of the thirty days he reached the river, but the ferry was on the other side and he could not cross. He called out to people across the water that he had come, but Shmuel ruled that this was not a return.

answer.actor: A man from Eretz Yisrael and Rabbi Hanina
answer.event: A man whose brother died childless in Bei Hoza'a asked Rabbi Hanina whether he could go down to Babylonia to perform levirate marriage.
answer.turn: Rabbi Hanina said the brother had left the Land to marry a 'Samaritan' and God had rightly killed him.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Hanina told him not to follow his brother out of the Land.
answer.summary: A man's brother had died childless, leaving a widow in far-off Bei Hoza'a in Babylonia. He asked Rabbi Hanina whether he should go there to marry her. Rabbi Hanina answered harshly that the brother had left the Land of Israel to marry a foreign woman, blessed be God who killed him, and asked whether this man wanted to follow him down.

answer.actor: A millstone owner and his renter
answer.event: A man rented his millstone to another in exchange for grinding services.
answer.turn: The owner got rich, bought his own millstone and donkey, and demanded money instead of grinding.
answer.summary: A man rented out his millstone, and the renter paid by grinding the owner's grain. Later the owner grew rich, bought a millstone and donkey of his own, and demanded rent in money. The renter refused, saying he had only agreed to grind.
answer.missing: The ruling or how the dispute ended; only Ravina's initial legal reasoning follows.

answer.event: A dying man said, 'My property goes to Toviya,' and after his death a man named Toviya came to claim it.
answer.turn: There was doubt whether this was the Toviya he meant.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan ruled 'Toviya has come,' and gave him the property.
answer.summary: A man on his deathbed said his property should go to Toviya. When he died, a Toviya came forward. Rabbi Yohanan ruled that the Toviya who came should get it, without worrying that a different Toviya was meant.

answer.actor: Mar Zutra and a rebellious wife
answer.event: A wife said she was disgusted with her husband, and Mar Zutra compelled her to stay with him.
answer.turn: From that couple came Rabbi Hanina of Sura.
answer.outcome: The Gemara says the good result was heavenly help and not a precedent.
answer.summary: A woman refused her husband, saying he disgusted her, and Mar Zutra forced her to remain married. The couple later had a son, the sage Rabbi Hanina of Sura. The Gemara cautions that this good outcome came from divine help and should not justify such coercion.

answer.actor: Rav Pappa and Rav Yitzhak son of Rav Yehuda
answer.event: At his son Abba Mar's wedding, Rav Pappa poured a cup for Rav Yitzhak, who did not stand for him.
answer.turn: Rav Pappa became angry.
answer.summary: Rav Pappa was serving drinks at his son Abba Mar's wedding. When he poured a cup for Rav Yitzhak son of Rav Yehuda, Rav Yitzhak did not rise before him, and Rav Pappa was offended.
answer.missing: Any response or resolution; the anecdote is cited only to make a legal point.

answer.event: Ravnai came to sell sesame and reported Shmuel's ruling that a witness and judge may combine.
answer.turn: Ameimar praised the ruling, and Rav Ashi retorted that he praised it only because his grandfather had, and that Rava had already refuted it.
answer.outcome: The ruling was rejected as refuted.
answer.summary: Ravnai, brother of Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba, came to sell sesame and quoted Shmuel's view that a witness and a judge can join together. Ameimar called it an excellent ruling. Rav Ashi mocked him for praising it just because his mother's father had, pointing out that Rava had already disproved it.
answer.missing: The exchange is mostly an argument over a ruling; little happens beyond the rebuke.

answer.event: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives, burdened with their stepmother's daily medical costs, asked his advice.
answer.turn: He told them to fix a lump sum with the doctor, so the cost would come out of her marriage settlement.
answer.outcome: He later regretted it, saying he had acted like a legal advisor, since an important person must not favor his relatives.
answer.summary: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives had to pay for their father's widow, who needed treatment every day. He advised them to agree a fixed fee with the doctor, which would shift the cost onto her marriage settlement. Afterward he regretted it, saying he had made himself like a lawyer coaching a party, which a man of his standing should not do.

answer.actor: Rav Aha bar Ya'akov and Rava
answer.event: Rav Aha bar Ya'akov allowed the freed sons of the maidservant Yudan to marry each other's former wives.
answer.turn: Rava challenged him that Rav Sheshet had forbidden it.
answer.outcome: Rav Aha replied that Rav Sheshet forbade it and he permitted it.
answer.summary: The sons of a maidservant named Yudan were freed, and Rav Aha bar Ya'akov permitted them to marry one another's wives. Rava objected that Rav Sheshet had prohibited this. Rav Aha answered simply that Rav Sheshet forbade it and he himself allowed it.
answer.missing: Whether the marriages took place; the incident is essentially a ruling and its challenge.

answer.actor: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
answer.event: The two sages were about to permit a nursing mother whose child was weaned or given to a wet nurse to remarry immediately, following a baraita.
answer.turn: An old woman told them Rav Nahman had forbidden exactly this in her own case, and Rav Pappi reminded them of Rabbi Meir's decree and Shmuel's ruling that the halakha follows Rabbi Meir's decrees.
answer.outcome: They admitted they had forgotten the principle, and the halakha was fixed: if the child died she may remarry, if weaned she may not.
answer.summary: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua planned to rule that a nursing mother who had given her child to a wet nurse could remarry at once. An old woman told them that when this happened to her, Rav Nahman forbade it. Rav Pappi then cited a baraita and Shmuel's principle that the halakha follows Rabbi Meir's protective decrees, and the two sages admitted they had forgotten it.

answer.actor: A depositor and the family of Rabbi Meyasha
answer.event: A man deposited seven pearls wrapped in a sheet with Rabbi Meyasha, who died without telling his household whose they were.
answer.turn: The dispute came before Rabbi Ami, who knew Rabbi Meyasha was not wealthy enough to own such pearls.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Ami awarded the pearls to the claimant, who had also given an identifying mark.
answer.summary: A man left seven pearls tied in a sheet at the house of Rabbi Meyasha, grandson of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi. Rabbi Meyasha died without saying whose they were, and the case came before Rabbi Ami. He ruled for the depositor, because he knew Rabbi Meyasha could not have afforded such gems and because the depositor described a distinguishing mark.

answer.actor: The daughter of Nakdimon ben Guryon
answer.event: The Sages allotted her four hundred gold coins a day for perfumes from her late husband's estate.
answer.turn: Instead of thanking them simply, she told them they should allot as much for their own daughters, a remark that could be heard as a blessing or as a jab.
answer.outcome: The Sages answered 'Amen.'
answer.summary: When the Sages set the perfume allowance for Nakdimon ben Guryon's widowed daughter at four hundred gold coins for that one day, she told them: may you pledge the same for your own daughters. The Sages answered after her, 'Amen.'

answer.actor: A man testifying before Rabbi Ami
answer.event: A man told Rabbi Ami that someone held presumptive status as a priest because he read first from the Torah.
answer.turn: Rabbi Ami questioned whether he read first as a priest or as a prominent scholar, and the witness answered that a Levite read after him.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Ami elevated the man to the priesthood on the witness's word.
answer.summary: A man came to Rabbi Ami and testified that another man was presumed to be a priest because he had been called first to the Torah. Rabbi Ami asked whether that might have been out of honor for a great scholar; the witness replied that a Levite was called right after him, which only happens after a priest. On that basis Rabbi Ami recognized him as a priest.

answer.actor: A man's daughter and his heirs
answer.event: A man willed a palm tree to his daughter, but the orphans divided the estate without giving her one.
answer.turn: Rav Yosef thought each heir could deflect her, as in the mishna, but Abaye objected that here the tree was owed by all of them together.
answer.outcome: Abaye ruled they must give her a palm tree and redivide the estate from the start.
answer.summary: A man left instructions that his daughter receive a palm tree, but his heirs split the property and left her with none. Rav Yosef first compared it to a case where each party can claim the obligation lies with someone else. Abaye disagreed, saying the tree was the shared obligation of all the heirs, and ruled that they must give her a tree and divide the estate again.

answer.actor: Two men whose lineage was mocked
answer.event: People called one man 'son of the Aramean woman' and another 'son of the Aramean man,' casting doubt on a parent's conversion.
answer.turn: Rav Asi and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi pointed out that the parent's later ritual immersions for purity counted as immersion for conversion.
answer.summary: One man was taunted as the son of an Aramean woman, implying his mother's conversion was invalid; Rav Asi answered that she had surely immersed for her menstrual purity. Another was taunted as the son of an Aramean man, and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi answered that the father had surely immersed after a seminal emission. Both immersions were taken as sufficient for conversion.
answer.missing: An explicit statement of how the cases ended (that the men were declared of unflawed lineage) is implied but not stated.

answer.event: A widow's son asked Rabbi Eliezer, and then Rabbi Yehoshua, whether to honor his father or mother first when both ask for water.
answer.turn: When he pressed Rabbi Yehoshua about a divorced mother, Rabbi Yehoshua saw from his tearful eyes that he was a widow's son with no father, so the question was idle.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Yehoshua answered him sarcastically: pour water in a basin and cluck at them like chickens.
answer.summary: A widow's son asked Rabbi Eliezer which parent to serve first if both asked for water; he was told the father, since the mother too must honor the father. Rabbi Yehoshua gave the same answer. When the young man asked what if the mother is divorced, Rabbi Yehoshua said his tear-filled eyes showed he was a widow's son and had no father, and mockingly told him to pour water in a basin and call them like chickens.

answer.event: When a man was presumed a priest because he read first from the Torah, Reish Lakish asked whether he had received teruma, and Rabbi Elazar objected; later the same case came before Rabbi Yohanan.
answer.turn: Rabbi Yohanan made exactly Rabbi Elazar's objection, revealing that Rabbi Elazar had been quoting him without attribution.
answer.outcome: Reish Lakish glared at Rabbi Elazar and rebuked him for repeating bar Nappaha's words without saying whose they were.
answer.summary: Reish Lakish once refused to accept a man as a priest on the basis of reading first from the Torah, asking whether he had received teruma at the threshing floor; Rabbi Elazar retorted that priesthood cannot depend on a threshing floor. Later, sitting before Rabbi Yohanan, the same kind of case came up and Rabbi Yohanan gave Rabbi Elazar's very answer. Reish Lakish looked sharply at Rabbi Elazar and complained that he had heard this from Rabbi Yohanan and not cited him.

answer.event: A man deposited sesame with a friend and later asked for it back.
answer.turn: The friend claimed the owner had already taken it; the owner described the amount and barrel, and the friend said the sesame there was different.
answer.summary: A man left sesame with a friend and later asked for it. The friend said he had already taken it back. The owner pointed to a barrel holding exactly the amount he had deposited, but the friend insisted that sesame was someone else's.
answer.missing: The ruling that resolved the dispute.

answer.actor: Rabbi Hiyya bar Ami's slave and a gentile woman
answer.event: Rabbi Hiyya bar Ami's slave had a gentile woman immerse so that he could have relations with her.
answer.turn: Rav Yosef said he could declare both her and her daughter fit to marry into Israel.
answer.summary: A slave of Rabbi Hiyya bar Ami had a gentile woman immerse for the sake of relations with him. Rav Yosef declared that he could rule both her and her daughter fit to marry Jews.
answer.missing: Whether he actually ruled so and the reasoning, which follows in later segments.

answer.event: Bonyos sent Rabbi an ancient se'a measure from Na'usa.
answer.outcome: Rabbi measured it and found it held 217 eggs.
answer.summary: Rav Dimi reported that a man named Bonyos sent Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi a se'a measure from Na'usa. Rabbi measured it and found that it held 217 eggs.

answer.event: Rabbi Banai held movable property belonging to orphans.
answer.turn: The orphan daughters came before Shmuel seeking support.
answer.outcome: Shmuel told Rabbi Banai to go and sustain them from it.
answer.summary: Rabbi Banai, brother of Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba, was holding movable property left by a dead man for his children. The orphan daughters brought the matter to Shmuel, who told Rabbi Banai to provide for them from that property.

answer.event: A gentile superintendent living near Rabbi Zeira refused to rent his domain to the neighbors for an eiruv.
answer.turn: The neighbors asked Rabbi Zeira whether they could rent it from his wife instead.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Zeira ruled, citing Rabbi Hanina, that a man's wife may establish an eiruv without his knowledge.
answer.summary: A gentile official lived in Rabbi Zeira's neighborhood and would not rent his domain to the Jewish neighbors so they could carry on Shabbat. They asked Rabbi Zeira whether renting from his wife would work. He answered with a teaching of Rabbi Hanina, via Reish Lakish, that a wife may make an eiruv without her husband knowing, so they could.

answer.actor: A man who sold his mother's ketubah rights
answer.event: A man sold his future rights to his mother's ketubah, stipulating he would not reimburse the buyer if his mother objected.
answer.turn: His mother died without objecting, and he himself contested the sale, claiming to stand in her place.
answer.outcome: Rava rejected the claim: he had at least guaranteed the sale against his own objections.
answer.summary: A man sold the rights to his mother's ketubah for a sum, telling the buyer he would not refund him if his mother objected. His mother died without objecting, and then he challenged the sale himself. Rami bar Hama thought he could object in his mother's place, but Rava said that even if he had not guaranteed against her objection, he had certainly guaranteed against his own.

answer.event: A bill of divorce was found in the flax house in Pumbedita.
answer.outcome: Rabba ruled on it in accordance with his own teaching.
answer.summary: A bill of divorce turned up in the flax house in Pumbedita, and Rabba issued a practical ruling on it according to his own halakhic view. Traditions differ on the details of where it was found and the circumstances.
answer.missing: What exactly Rabba ruled (whether the get was returned) is not stated in the passage itself.

answer.event: Ben Azzai taught that one who does not procreate is like one who sheds blood, yet he himself never married.
answer.turn: His colleagues confronted him: he expounds well but does not practice what he preaches.
answer.outcome: Ben Azzai replied that his soul yearned for Torah and the world could be sustained by others.
answer.summary: After Ben Azzai taught how grave it is not to have children, the sages pointed out that he preached well but did not live by it, since he had never married. Ben Azzai answered that his soul longed for Torah, and that the world could be populated through others.

answer.event: A large unenclosed yard in Pum Nahara opened on one side to the town and on the other to a vineyard path ending at a riverbank, and the sages sought a way to permit carrying in it.
answer.turn: Abaye rejected a partition on the riverbank and a doorframe the camels would knock down, then proposed a side post at the vineyard path, which Rava rejected as misleading.
answer.outcome: Rava proposed instead a side post at the yard's opening to the town.
answer.summary: In Pum Nahara there was a yard where carrying on Shabbat was a problem. Abaye considered and rejected a partition on the riverbank and a doorframe that passing camels would knock over, then suggested a side post at the vineyard path. Rava objected that people would wrongly think a side post works for any vineyard path, and suggested placing it at the opening to the town instead.
answer.missing: Whether either solution was actually implemented.
The incident referred to (at the wagons of Tzippori) is only located, not narrated, in the shown text.

answer.actor: Rav Avya and his wife, the sister of Rami bar Hama
answer.event: Her marriage contract was lost and the couple came before Rav Yosef to ask what to do.
answer.turn: Rav Yosef first said the Rabbis allow a man to live with his wife for years without a contract, but Abaye objected that the halakha follows Rabbi Meir's decrees.
answer.outcome: Rav Yosef told them to go and write her a new marriage contract.
answer.summary: Rav Avya was married to the sister of Rami bar Hama, and her marriage contract was lost. They asked Rav Yosef, who cited the view that a man may go two or three years without one. Abaye objected that the law follows Rabbi Meir, who is strict about this. Rav Yosef then told them to go and write her a new contract.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yohanan and Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat
answer.event: Rabbi Elazar silenced Rabbi Yohanan with an objection to his teaching about burning leftover sacrificial meat.
answer.turn: Rabbi Yohanan praised the exposition as if from Moses, but Reish Lakish revealed it was really a baraita from Torat Kohanim.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan went and learned Torat Kohanim in three days and mastered it in three months.
answer.summary: Rabbi Yohanan was teaching when Rabbi Elazar raised an objection from a baraita, and Rabbi Yohanan had no answer. Afterwards he told Reish Lakish that Ben Pedat expounded like Moses receiving the Torah from God. Reish Lakish said it was not his own idea but a baraita in Torat Kohanim. Rabbi Yohanan then learned that whole work in three days and understood it in three months.

answer.actor: a tumtum (person of indeterminate sex) in the town of Biri
answer.event: He was operated on so that his genitals were opened, and he later fathered seven children.
answer.turn: The case is cited against Rabbi Yehuda, who would reply that the children's paternity is doubtful.
answer.summary: A person of indeterminate sex living in Biri was seated for an operation and had his genitals opened, and he later had seven children. Rabbi Ami cites the case to challenge Rabbi Yehuda's view that such a person is impotent; Rabbi Yehuda's answer would be to question where the children came from.
answer.missing: The case is only cited as an argument; nothing further happens to the man in the text.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yosei bar Avin (or Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Zevida), and Ameimar
answer.event: A visiting sage ruled on the status of children born to women who had relations with a slave.
answer.turn: The reports disagree on who the sage was and whether he declared the married woman's child unfit.
answer.outcome: Ameimar, on a visit, declared such children fit in both cases.
answer.summary: Rav Gazza reported that a visiting sage once ruled the child of an unmarried woman and a slave fit to marry, but the child of a married woman unfit. Another version says the visitor was a different sage who ruled both children fit. Ameimar, visiting another town, also ruled both fit.
answer.missing: The incidents are reported only as rulings; no details of the people involved.

answer.actor: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda, Marei bar Mar, Rav Huna and his son Rabba
answer.event: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda sent Marei bar Mar to ask Rav Huna whether the halakha follows Rabbi Elazar on bills of divorce.
answer.turn: Before the question arrived, Rav Huna died.
answer.outcome: Rav Huna's son Rabba answered in his father's name that the halakha follows Rabbi Elazar.
answer.summary: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda sent a request to Marei bar Mar to ask Rav Huna a legal question about bills of divorce. In the meantime Rav Huna died. His son Rabba answered instead, reporting that his father, and other learned teachers in Rav's name, held that the halakha follows Rabbi Elazar.

answer.actor: a man who left a dowry to his daughter, and his heirs
answer.event: A man's will instructed his heirs to give his daughter a dowry, and dowry prices then fell.
answer.turn: The question arose who gets the difference between the intended and the actual cost.
answer.outcome: Rav Idi bar Avin ruled the saving goes to the male orphans.
answer.summary: A man instructed his heirs to give his daughter a dowry, but before it was given the cost of dowries dropped. Rav Idi bar Avin ruled that the money saved belongs to the sons, not the daughter.
answer.missing: Only the legal facts and ruling are given; no further development.

answer.actor: a woman holding a bag of documents
answer.event: Heirs demanded a bag of documents deposited with her, and she claimed she had seized it from the deceased while he was alive.
answer.turn: Rav Nahman asked for witnesses that the deceased had demanded it in his lifetime and she refused, and she had none.
answer.outcome: He ruled her seizure was after death and therefore worthless.
answer.summary: A woman had a bag of documents deposited with her, and after the owner died his heirs claimed it. She said she had seized it during his lifetime to cover a debt. Rav Nahman asked if she had witnesses that the owner had demanded it while alive and she refused; she had none, so he ruled it counted as seizure after death, which is invalid.

answer.actor: a man in love with a woman (reported in a letter from Rabba's brothers)
answer.event: A man suffering from love for a woman wanted to leave the Land of Israel to be with her.
answer.turn: He heard the teaching about the importance of living in the Land of Israel.
answer.outcome: He stayed and suffered until the day he died.
answer.summary: Rabba's brothers wrote to him from the Land of Israel, quoting Ilfa's story of a man who was suffering for love of a woman and wished to leave the land. When he heard how important it is to stay in the Land of Israel, he stayed and endured his suffering until he died. The rest of the letter urges Rabba to come and gives health advice.
answer.missing: The anecdote is told in a few words; the rest of the passage is advice, not narrative.

answer.actor: an unmarried man who came before Rav Nahman
answer.event: A man claimed before Rav Nahman that he found his bride's virginity absent.
answer.turn: Rav Nahman realized that an inexperienced bachelor could only know this from consorting with prostitutes.
answer.outcome: He ordered the man flogged with palm branches.
answer.summary: A man who had never been married came to Rav Nahman and claimed that his new wife was not a virgin. Rav Nahman reasoned that he could only know this if he had been with prostitutes. He ordered that the man be flogged with palm branches.

answer.event: Rabbi Tavla visited Mehoza and saw a door bolt hanging beside the door, not tied to it.
answer.turn: He said nothing against it.
answer.summary: Rabbi Tavla came to Mehoza and saw a door bolt hanging from the side of a door. He made no objection to the people there. The Gemara explains that this bolt could be lifted by its rope.
answer.missing: The incident is cited only as a legal precedent; there is no development or ending.

answer.actor: a woman selling belts and a man who snatched one
answer.event: A man grabbed a belt from a woman selling them and asked if she would be betrothed to him if he gave it back.
answer.turn: She took the belt and said nothing.
answer.outcome: Rav Nahman ruled she was not betrothed, since she could say she was only taking back her own property.
answer.summary: A woman was selling belts when a man snatched one from her. When she demanded it back, he asked whether she would be betrothed to him if he returned it. She took it in silence. Rav Nahman ruled that her silence meant nothing, because she was simply taking back what was hers.

answer.actor: the wife (widow) of Rav Yosef son of Rava
answer.event: She came before Rav Nehemya asking him to set her allowance for food and then for wine.
answer.turn: He granted wine, explaining that the people of Mehoza drink wine.
answer.outcome: She received both sustenance and wine.
answer.summary: The wife of Rav Yosef son of Rava came before Rav Nehemya and asked him to fix her food allowance, which he did. She then asked for wine as well. He granted it, saying he knew the people of Mehoza drink wine.

answer.event: Rabbi Hiyya and Bar Kappara each jumped up and swore by the Temple service that they had heard opposite rulings from Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.
answer.turn: Unable to settle it by tradition, each began to argue it by reasoning, and the same clash repeated over three cases.
answer.summary: Rabbi Hiyya and Bar Kappara disagreed about how many counts a person is liable for in several Temple cases. Each leapt up and swore by the Temple service that he had heard his version from Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi. Each then argued his view from reasoning, and the scene repeated for three different cases. The rest is the Gemara's legal analysis of their dispute.
answer.missing: The confrontation has no resolution; the text moves into legal analysis.

answer.actor: the Israelites after the war with Midian
answer.event: To tell which captive girls were of age, they passed them before the High Priest's frontplate.
answer.turn: The faces of those who were of age miraculously turned pale.
answer.summary: The Gemara asks how the Israelites knew which Midianite girls were of age. Rabbi Shimon Hasida explains that they were passed before the High Priest's frontplate, and those whose faces turned pale were known to be of age.
answer.missing: This is an explanatory gloss on a biblical episode; the episode itself is not told.

answer.event: Nehemya was so absorbed in his learning that he walked beyond the Shabbat boundary.
answer.turn: Rav Hisda told Rav Nahman his student was stuck and in distress.
answer.outcome: Rav Nahman said to form a partition of people so he could walk back in.
answer.summary: Nehemya, son of Rav Hanilai, was so engrossed in his studies on Shabbat that he wandered past the boundary he was allowed to walk. Rav Hisda told Rav Nahman that his student was stuck outside. Rav Nahman told him to line people up to form a human wall so Nehemya could walk back inside it.

answer.actor: Rav and Rabba bar bar Hana
answer.event: Rabba bar bar Hana gave Rav money to buy a piece of land for him, and Rav bought it for himself.
answer.turn: The land lay in a valley of violent men who respected Rav but not Rabba bar bar Hana, so only Rav could buy it.
answer.outcome: Rav bought it without telling him first, fearing someone else would buy it in the meantime.
answer.summary: Rabba bar bar Hana gave Rav money to buy a certain plot of land for him, but Rav bought it for himself. The land was in a valley of violent men who would deal respectfully with Rav but not with Rabba bar bar Hana. Rav did not stop to tell him first, worried that someone else would snap it up in the meantime.

answer.actor: Yehuda bar Mareimar, Rav Pappa, and Abba of Sura
answer.event: Rav Pappa pressed Yehuda bar Mareimar to come into the house of Abba of Sura while his son's marriage contract was being written.
answer.turn: Yehuda's silent presence made Abba of Sura think he was angry, so Abba signed away everything he owned as dowry.
answer.outcome: Abba offered to retract, but Yehuda told him not to become a man who goes back on his word.
answer.summary: Rav Pappa went to have his son's marriage contract written at the house of Abba of Sura, and Yehuda bar Mareimar came out to escort him but would not go in, fearing his presence would pressure the bride's father into a larger dowry. Rav Pappa forced him to enter; Yehuda sat in silence, and Abba of Sura, thinking he was angry, wrote all his property into the dowry and begged him to speak. Yehuda said he had never wanted this; when Abba offered to retract, Yehuda told him not to make himself a man who goes back on his word.

answer.event: A superintendent refused to rent his domain to his neighbors for an eiruv, so they sought a ruling on renting it from his wife.
answer.turn: Rav Yehuda bar Oshaya and Rav Mattana had no answer.
answer.outcome: Rav Yehuda told them, citing Shmuel, that a man's wife may establish an eiruv without his knowledge.
answer.summary: A superintendent living near Rav Yehuda bar Oshaya would not rent his domain to his neighbors so they could carry on Shabbat. They asked Rav Yehuda bar Oshaya, then Rav Mattana, whether they could rent it from his wife, and neither knew. Finally Rav Yehuda told them in Shmuel's name that a man's wife may establish an eiruv without his knowledge.

answer.event: Minyamin, a first-generation Egyptian convert, married another first-generation Egyptian convert.
answer.outcome: He planned to marry his son to a second-generation Egyptian convert so his grandson could enter the congregation.
answer.summary: Rabbi Yehuda recalled his friend Minyamin, an Egyptian convert among Rabbi Akiva's students. Minyamin said he had married a fellow first-generation Egyptian convert and intended to marry his son to a second-generation one, so that his grandson would be permitted to marry into the community.
answer.missing: Whether the planned marriage happened; the passage is mostly a reported statement of intent.

answer.actor: Rabbi Abba bar Shumni and Rav Menashya bar Yirmeya
answer.event: Two sages parting at the ford of the Yofti River agreed each would tell the other a teaching he had not heard.
answer.outcome: One defined the difference between someone who has drunk and someone who is drunk; the other taught what one who seizes a convert's property should do to keep it.
answer.summary: Rabbi Abba bar Shumni and Rav Menashya bar Yirmeya were taking leave of each other at a river crossing, and agreed each would share a teaching the other had not heard, since parting over a point of law keeps a friend in mind. One explained that a man who has drunk can still speak before a king, while a drunk man cannot. The other taught that whoever takes possession of a dead convert's property should buy a Torah scroll with it so the rest stays with him.
answer.missing: The narrative frame has little turn; the actual parting is implied, not shown.

answer.event: Levi publicly taught Rabbi's ruling that a bill of divorce written on forbidden items is valid, citing Rabbi by name.
answer.turn: The audience did not praise him.
answer.outcome: When he taught it in the name of the majority, they praised him.
answer.summary: Levi went out and taught Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's ruling that a bill of divorce written on items forbidden for benefit is valid, giving it in Rabbi's name, and his listeners did not praise him. When he taught it as the view of the many, they praised him, showing that the law follows that ruling.

answer.missing: Only a question to an elder about when a woman was permitted to remarry; the incident itself and any answer are not given.

answer.actor: Rav Pappa and Pappa the ox herder
answer.event: Rav Pappa instructed that the name of Pappa the ox herder, who could not sign, be written in saliva for him to trace in ink.
answer.summary: Pappa the ox herder could not sign his name as a witness. Rav Pappa ruled that his name should be written for him in saliva so he could trace over it in ink.
answer.missing: Little more than a reported ruling; no turn or outcome is told.

answer.event: Rabbi Yohanan's students gathered huge quantities of Genosar fruit for him, and he ate it all.
answer.turn: After eating so much he swore he had not tasted anything nourishing.
answer.outcome: The Gemara corrects his words to 'sustaining food', since fruit does nourish.
answer.summary: Rabba bar bar Hana recalled following Rabbi Yohanan to eat the sweet fruit of Genosar, gathering so much that every hundred fruits would overflow a three-se'a basket. Rabbi Yohanan ate them all and then swore he had still not tasted anything nourishing. The Gemara amends his words to say he had not eaten real sustaining food.

answer.event: Ravina examined a slaughterer's knife in Babylonia during the lifetime of his teacher Rav Ashi, who challenged him.
answer.turn: Ravina cited Rav Hamnuna's precedent; Rav Ashi denied it; Ravina reconciled both versions.
answer.outcome: Ravina argued that as Rav Ashi's disciple-colleague he too was permitted to rule.
answer.summary: Ravina checked a slaughterer's knife in Babylonia while his teacher Rav Ashi was alive, and Rav Ashi asked why he had done so. Ravina pointed to Rav Hamnuna, who had ruled in Harta De'argez in Rav Hisda's lifetime; Rav Ashi replied the tradition was that Rav Hamnuna had not ruled. Ravina answered that both traditions were true: Rav Hamnuna had not ruled under his main teacher Rav Huna, but did rule under Rav Hisda, whose disciple-colleague he was, and Ravina claimed the same standing with Rav Ashi.
answer.missing: Rav Ashi's response to Ravina's final argument.

answer.event: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi ruled (or meant to rule) in a case according to the Rabbis of the mishna.
answer.turn: Perata objected that this would leave the court no more power than an ordinary person.
answer.outcome: Rabbi reversed his ruling (in Rav Safra's version, did not act on it).
answer.summary: Rav Dimi reported that in a certain case Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi ruled according to the Rabbis of the mishna. Perata, grandson of Rabbi Perata the Great, objected that the court would then have no advantage over an ordinary person, and Rabbi reversed his decision. In Rav Safra's version, Rabbi only intended to rule that way and, after Perata's objection, did not.

answer.missing: Describes Rav Huna's habitual practice with litigants, not a single event.
A request, a habit and a ruling about orla; no event unfolds.

answer.event: People asked Rabbi Elai where Rabbi Abbahu was hiding.
answer.outcome: He answered in riddling language that Abbahu had consulted the Nasi and gone south to the sages there.
answer.summary: People asked Rabbi Elai to show them where Rabbi Abbahu was hiding. Rabbi Elai answered in a riddle: Abbahu had taken counsel with 'the one who crowns' (the Nasi) and gone south to 'Mephibosheth', meaning the southern sages.
answer.missing: Why Rabbi Abbahu was hiding and what happened afterward.

answer.actor: Ravina and the daughter of Rav Ashi
answer.event: Ravina collected the dowry share for Rav Ashi's daughter from two heirs.
answer.turn: From Mar son of Rav Ashi she got intermediate land with no oath, but from the orphan grandson she got inferior land with an oath.
answer.summary: Ravina arranged for Rav Ashi's daughter to receive her tenth of the estate. From her brother Mar son of Rav Ashi she took intermediate-quality land without an oath, but from her orphaned nephew she took only inferior land and had to swear an oath.
answer.missing: Mainly a legal precedent; no turn or outcome beyond the ruling.

answer.event: Rava bar Avuh collected money on two promissory notes in Mehoza naming Havai bar Nanai and Nanai bar Havai.
answer.summary: Two promissory notes surfaced in Mehoza naming Havai bar Nanai and Nanai bar Havai, names that were common there. Rava bar Avuh collected the debts on them anyway, without worrying that they might belong to others of the same name.
answer.missing: Only a case cited as legal proof; the rest is argument.

answer.event: A man gave Shmuel a hand as he stepped off a ferry.
answer.turn: Shmuel learned the man had a case to bring before him.
answer.outcome: Shmuel declared himself disqualified from judging the man's case.
answer.summary: Shmuel was crossing a river by ferry when a man gave him a hand getting out. Shmuel asked what he was doing there, and the man said he had a case for him to judge. Shmuel told him that this small favor disqualified him from hearing the case.

answer.event: Rav Beivai told the sages not to listen to Rav Yosef's attribution of a ruling to Rabbi.
answer.turn: Beivai revealed he had taught it to Yosef himself, in the name of Rav Adda bar Ahava, and the word was 'many' (rabbim), not 'Rabbi'.
answer.outcome: Rav Yosef exclaimed that he had mistaken 'Rabbi' for 'many'.
answer.summary: When Rav Yosef cited a ruling as taught by Rabbi, Rav Beivai told the sages not to listen: he had taught it to Rav Yosef himself, in the name of Rav Adda bar Ahava, and it spoke of 'many' in the outer courtyard. Rav Yosef exclaimed 'Master of Abraham!' and admitted he had confused 'Rabbi' with 'rabbim'.
answer.missing: Why Rav Yosef forgot (an illness is mentioned only in the translator's gloss).

answer.actor: Rabbi Meir and a man who made an onion eiruv
answer.event: A man told Rabbi Meir in Ardiska that he had made his eiruv with onions in order to walk to Tiv'in.
answer.turn: Rabbi Meir held the onion eiruv invalid, so the man was outside his Shabbat limit.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Meir made him stay within his four cubits.
answer.summary: Rabbi Meir was spending Shabbat in Ardiska when a man came and told him he had made his eiruv with onions so he could walk to Tiv'in. Rabbi Meir held that onions do not make a valid eiruv, so the man had already left his Shabbat limit, and he ordered him to stay within his four cubits.

answer.event: Rav Hisda's daughter asked her father, who studied through the night, whether he would not sleep a little.
answer.outcome: He replied that long days with little chance to study would soon come, and then he would sleep plenty.
answer.summary: Rav Hisda spent his nights studying, and his daughter asked if he did not want to sleep a little. He answered that the long days in which no Torah can be studied would come soon enough, meaning death, and then he would sleep a great deal.

answer.event: Rabbi Elazar taught that the unlearned will not be resurrected, and his teacher Rabbi Yohanan objected that God is not pleased by such a statement.
answer.turn: Seeing Rabbi Yohanan grieved, Rabbi Elazar searched for and found a remedy for the unlearned.
answer.outcome: He taught that one who marries his daughter to a scholar or supports scholars is credited as cleaving to the Divine Presence, and so merits life.
answer.summary: Rabbi Elazar taught that ordinary uneducated people would not rise at the resurrection. His teacher Rabbi Yohanan protested that God would not be pleased to hear this said of them, and Rabbi Elazar defended it from another verse. But seeing how distressed Rabbi Yohanan was, Rabbi Elazar told him he had found a remedy: whoever marries his daughter to a scholar, or does business for scholars, or benefits them from his property, is considered as cleaving to God and so lives.

answer.event: The priestly court set widows' marriage contracts at one hundred dinars, then raised them to two hundred when widows were demeaned.
answer.turn: Grooms then stopped marrying priestly widows in favor of Israelite virgins at the same price.
answer.outcome: The court restored the original amount.
answer.summary: The priestly court originally fixed a marriage contract of 400 dinars for a virgin and 100 for a widow. When they saw widows being treated with contempt they raised the widow's sum to 200, but then men avoided priestly widows, preferring to marry an Israelite virgin for the same price, so the court restored the old amounts. It is an institutional history rather than a story about particular people.

answer.actor: Rav Aha son of Rav Avya
answer.event: Rav Aha met Rav Ashi's students and asked whether their master had said anything about the doorway-form.
answer.outcome: They told him Rav Ashi had said nothing.
answer.summary: Rav Aha, son of Rav Avya, came upon Rav Ashi's students and asked whether Rav Ashi had taught anything about the form of a doorway. They answered that he had said nothing at all.
answer.missing: Any consequence of the exchange; it is a brief encounter serving a legal point.

answer.event: A case arose in Rav Hisda's study hall, which Rav Hisda brought to Rav Huna's study hall.
answer.outcome: They resolved it from a mishna about an agent and consecrated property.
answer.summary: An actual case came up in Rav Hisda's study hall; he brought it to Rav Huna's, and there they settled it by citing a mishna about an owner who tells his agent to fetch an item. The case itself is only gestured at; the rest is legal reasoning.
answer.missing: The facts of the incident itself are not described.

answer.event: Rabban Gamliel's daughter was married to his brother Abba.
answer.turn: Abba died childless.
answer.outcome: Rabban Gamliel took his brother's other wife, his daughter's rival wife, in levirate marriage.
answer.summary: Rabban Gamliel's daughter was married to his brother Abba, who also had another wife. Abba died without children, and Rabban Gamliel performed levirate marriage with the other wife, his daughter's co-wife. The Gemara then debates what this case proves.

answer.event: A woman named Me'oret made her slave perform three of the dangerous actions in sequence.
answer.outcome: The slave died.
answer.summary: A woman named Me'oret made her slave do three of the six dangerous acts, such as travel, bloodletting and bathing, and he died. The Gemara cites it only to argue about whether doing them out of order is fatal.
answer.missing: Why she did it and any details of the episode.

answer.event: Rabbi Yosei met Elijah the prophet and asked him how a wife helps her husband.
answer.outcome: Elijah answered that she turns his raw wheat and flax into bread and clothing, lighting his eyes and standing him on his feet.
answer.summary: Rabbi Yosei encountered Elijah the prophet and asked him what the verse means when it calls a wife a helper. Elijah replied that a man brings home raw wheat and flax, which he cannot eat or wear as they are; his wife transforms them, and so she brightens his eyes and sets him on his feet.

answer.actor: Rav Nahman bar Rav Hisda and Rabba
answer.event: A bill of divorce dated by the governor of Bascar came up, and Rav Nahman bar Rav Hisda sent the question to Rabba.
answer.outcome: Rabba replied that even Rabbi Meir would accept it, since the governor belongs to the kingdom.
answer.summary: A divorce document turned up dated by the years of the governor of Bascar rather than the king. Rav Nahman bar Rav Hisda sent the question to Rabba, who ruled that it was valid even by Rabbi Meir's strict view, because the governor is an official of that same kingdom.

answer.event: A dying Madonite wished to give away his many movable goods as gifts.
answer.turn: The Sages told him the only way was to transfer them by means of land, so he bought a small rocky plot near Jerusalem.
answer.outcome: He assigned the land with the sheep and barrels to a recipient, died, and the Sages carried out his wishes.
answer.summary: A man from Madon living in Jerusalem had a great deal of movable property and, when ill, wanted to give it away. The Sages told him the only remedy was to transfer it along with land, so he bought a rocky plot near Jerusalem and declared that its northern part, with a hundred sheep and a hundred barrels, went to a certain person. He died, and the Sages upheld his gift.

answer.actor: Rava and Rav Mari bar Rahel
answer.event: Rava declared Rav Mari bar Rahel, son of a gentile father and Jewish mother, fit to marry into Israel.
answer.outcome: Rava appointed him one of the officials of Babylonia.
answer.summary: Rav Mari bar Rahel was the son of a gentile father and a Jewish mother. Rava ruled that his lineage was unflawed and even appointed him an official in Babylonia, reasoning that because his mother was Jewish he counted as one 'from among your brethren'.

answer.event: When the exiles returned from Babylonia they camped by a particular well.
answer.outcome: The prophets among them permitted drawing from it on a Festival, following an ancestral custom.
answer.summary: When the exiles came back from Babylonia they camped beside one particular well, and the prophets among them allowed them to draw water from it on a Festival. The Gemara adds that this was really an inherited custom that the prophets let them continue.
answer.missing: Little actual event beyond the encampment; it explains a custom.

answer.event: Rava publicly taught that one may scatter straw on a muddy courtyard on Shabbat in the ordinary way.
answer.turn: Rav Pappa challenged him with a baraita requiring an unusual manner.
answer.outcome: Rava appointed a speaker and publicly announced that his teaching had been a mistake.
answer.summary: Rava taught that a courtyard turned muddy by rain on Shabbat may be covered with straw. Rav Pappa objected with a baraita saying the straw may only be scattered with the bottom of a broken basket. Rava then set up a public speaker and announced that what he had said was his own mistake, restating the correct rule in Rabbi Eliezer's name.

answer.event: In high spirits Abaye declared himself ready like ben Azzai to answer any question.
answer.turn: One of the Sages challenged him on why he read the slave-redemption verses leniently.
answer.outcome: Abaye answered that the Torah is lenient toward the Hebrew slave; the debate continues.
answer.summary: Abaye once boasted that he was like ben Azzai in the markets of Tiberias, ready to answer anything. A scholar promptly tested him: why interpret the verses on redeeming a Hebrew slave leniently rather than stringently? Abaye replied that the Torah shows concern for the slave's welfare, and the exchange turns into an extended legal argument with no clear end.
answer.missing: The end of the exchange; it continues as legal discussion past the passage.

answer.event: Visiting Neharde'a, Rav Avya saw a man tying a door bolt with a reed.
answer.outcome: He ruled that this door may not be locked with that bolt on Shabbat.
answer.summary: When Rav Avya came to Neharde'a he saw a man fastening a bolt to a door with a reed. He declared that the door could not be locked with it on Shabbat, since the bolt was not properly attached.

answer.event: In a shepherds' village an inlet of the sea broke through a courtyard wall.
answer.outcome: The case came before Rav Yehuda, who required only a single board to permit carrying.
answer.summary: Rav Yosef recalled an incident in a shepherds' village where a narrow inlet of the sea had breached an entire wall of a courtyard. The case was brought to Rav Yehuda, who ruled that one upright board was enough to keep the courtyard permitted.

answer.event: Abaye posed a difficulty to Rav Dimi about Rabbi Yohanan's view, and Rav Dimi fell silent.
answer.turn: Abaye himself proposed the answer.
answer.outcome: Rav Dimi praised him, saying it was as if Abaye had been present when Rabbi Yohanan taught it.
answer.summary: Abaye challenged Rav Dimi with a contradiction in Rabbi Yohanan's rulings, and Rav Dimi had no answer. Abaye then suggested the resolution himself: the Egyptian convert's case depends on a verse that ties status to birth. Rav Dimi exclaimed that he had seen Abaye's head among the pillars when Rabbi Yohanan taught this, praising him as though he had been there.

answer.event: Throughout Rav Huna's lifetime Rav Hisda was asked even about cooking an egg in a dairy dish.
answer.outcome: He refused to rule, out of deference to his teacher.
answer.summary: As long as his teacher Rav Huna was alive, Rav Hisda declined to issue rulings, even on a question as simple as cooking an egg in a dairy dish. It is cited as a pattern of conduct rather than a single episode.
answer.missing: A single concrete occasion; it describes ongoing behavior.

answer.event: The Sages urged Rabbi Abba bar Zavda to marry and have children.
answer.turn: He replied that if he deserved children he would have had them from his first wife, but the real reason was revealed: he had become impotent from Rav Huna's long lectures.
answer.outcome: He put the Sages off with an excuse and did not remarry.
answer.summary: The Sages told Rabbi Abba bar Zavda to take a wife and have children. He answered that had he been worthy he would already have had children from his first wife. The Gemara explains that this was only an excuse: he had in fact become impotent from holding himself back during Rav Huna's lengthy discourses.

answer.event: Nearly blind in old age, Rav Yehuda struggled to read documents before signing them.
answer.turn: Ulla told him it was unnecessary, since great authorities had scribes read documents to them.
answer.summary: Rav Yehuda, whose sight was failing, went to great effort to read documents himself before signing them. Ulla told him he need not, because Rabbi Elazar in the Land of Israel and Rav Nahman had court scribes read documents aloud to them before they signed. The Gemara adds limits on when this is allowed.
answer.missing: Whether Rav Yehuda followed the advice.

answer.actor: Shmuel's father and Rabbi Yehuda Nesia
answer.event: A bill of divorce signed by one Androlinai of Neharde'a was found, and Shmuel's father sent the question of its validity to Rabbi Yehuda Nesia.
answer.turn: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia, rather than accepting it, replied that all of Neharde'a must be searched for another man of that name.
answer.outcome: The instruction to search is given; the result of the search is not told.
answer.summary: A bill of divorce turned up in Neharde'a, signed by a man named Androlinai, and it was unclear whether it was really from the woman's husband. Shmuel's father sent the question to Rabbi Yehuda Nesia in the Land of Israel. He wrote back that the whole city must be checked for another man with the same name.
answer.missing: What the search found and whether the woman was permitted to remarry.

answer.event: Ameimar permitted Rav Huna bar Natan to marry a woman from Mehoza.
answer.turn: Rav Ashi challenged him, pointing out that three academies did not teach the lenient tradition he seemed to rely on.
answer.outcome: Ameimar did not accept the objection, because he had heard the ruling directly from Rav Zevid of Neharde'a.
answer.summary: Ameimar allowed Rav Huna bar Natan to marry a woman from Mehoza, a town of doubtful lineage. Rav Ashi questioned him, noting that the schools of Rav Kahana, Rav Pappa and Rav Zevid did not teach the tradition that would allow it. Ameimar held his ground, because he had heard the ruling in person from Rav Zevid of Neharde'a.

answer.event: Ulla praised Rav Hamnuna's learning but lamented that he came from Harpanya, a town of flawed lineage.
answer.turn: Rav Hamnuna was ashamed, and Ulla asked him where he paid his poll tax.
answer.outcome: When he answered Pum Nahara, Ulla declared that he was therefore from Pum Nahara and his lineage was sound.
answer.summary: Rav Hamnuna was studying before Ulla, who exclaimed what a great man he was, if only he were not from Harpanya, a town known for flawed lineage. Rav Hamnuna was humiliated. Ulla then asked where he paid his poll tax, and when he said Pum Nahara, Ulla concluded that he belonged to Pum Nahara and his lineage was not in question.

answer.event: Judges ruled a case following Rabbi Tarfon, and Reish Lakish overturned their decision.
answer.turn: Rabbi Yohanan criticized him for treating the error as if it were a matter of Torah law.
answer.outcome: The rebuke is given; whether the reversal stood is not said.
answer.summary: Some judges decided an inheritance case following Rabbi Tarfon's view, and Reish Lakish reversed their ruling and returned the money. Rabbi Yohanan rebuked him, saying he had acted as though the judges had erred in Torah law, where a mistaken ruling must be undone.
answer.missing: How the matter was resolved after Rabbi Yohanan's criticism.

answer.event: Rabbi Zeira, who in Babylonia had believed the Rabbis disagreed with Rabbi's rule, went up to the Land of Israel and found Rabbi Asi teaching otherwise.
answer.turn: Rabbi Asi taught in Rabbi Yohanan's name that all agree with the rule, and the dispute concerned a different formula.
answer.outcome: His earlier understanding is corrected; nothing further happens.
answer.summary: In Babylonia, Rabbi Zeira and his colleagues assumed the Rabbis disputed a ruling about conditions. When he moved to the Land of Israel he found Rabbi Asi teaching, in Rabbi Yohanan's name, that everyone agrees with that ruling and the disagreement is only about saying 'from today and after my death'.
answer.missing: Little action beyond hearing a teaching; it is mainly a report of a tradition.

answer.event: Judges in Neharde'a and Rav Hana bar Bizna in Pumbedita ordered daughters supported from movable property.
answer.turn: Rav Nahman ordered them to reverse their rulings, threatening to seize their houses otherwise.
answer.outcome: The threat is issued; whether they complied is not told.
answer.summary: Courts in Neharde'a and Pumbedita ruled that a dead man's daughters should be supported from his movable property, and Rav Hana bar Bizna collected the money. Rav Nahman told the judges to reverse their decisions, or he would take their own houses to repay those they had ruled against.
answer.missing: Whether the judges reversed their rulings.

answer.event: A man told witnesses that if he did not marry his betrothed by the New Moon of Adar, his document would be a bill of divorce.
answer.turn: When Adar arrived he claimed he had said Nisan.
answer.outcome: The text turns to legal analysis; no ruling or outcome for the couple is given.
answer.summary: A man set a condition that his bill of divorce would take effect if he did not marry his fiancee by the New Moon of Adar. When the date came and he had not married her, he claimed he had actually said Nisan. The Gemara then analyzes what legal concern might apply, without telling how the case ended.
answer.missing: The ruling or outcome of the case.

answer.event: Rabbi Yehoshua went to study with Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri and found him sitting among trees.
answer.turn: Rabbi Yehoshua stretched a vine between two trees and asked whether one could sow seeds on the other side.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri answered that it is permitted if the trees are ten cubits apart and forbidden if more.
answer.summary: Although he was already an expert in the laws of mixed planting, Rabbi Yehoshua went to learn from Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri. Finding him among the trees, he stretched a vine from one tree to another and asked whether seeds could be sown beyond it. Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri ruled that it is allowed if the trees are up to ten cubits apart, and forbidden if farther.

answer.actor: a man in Rabbi Ami's neighborhood
answer.event: Rabbi Ami publicly declared a neighbor to be a mamzer.
answer.turn: The man went about weeping.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Ami told him that by declaring it he had given him life.
answer.summary: A man living near Rabbi Ami was publicly declared by him to be a mamzer, of illegitimate birth. The man went around crying over it. Rabbi Ami told him that he had in fact given him life, since a known mamzer is not struck down from Heaven.

answer.event: Rabbi once ruled in a case following Rabbi Elazar's opinion.
answer.turn: Afterward he remembered that Rabbi Elazar's view was contested.
answer.outcome: He said Rabbi Elazar is worthy to rely on in a pressing situation.
answer.summary: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi once decided a case according to Rabbi Elazar. Later he recalled that Rabbi Elazar's colleagues disagreed with him. Rather than retract, he said that Rabbi Elazar is a fit authority to rely on in times of need.

answer.actor: Rabbi Elazar ben Tzadok and his family
answer.event: One year the Ninth of Av fell on Shabbat, so the family of Sena'av ben Binyamin postponed the fast to Sunday.
answer.turn: Sunday was their family festival.
answer.outcome: They fasted but did not complete the fast.
answer.summary: Rabbi Elazar ben Tzadok recalled that his family, descendants of Sena'av ben Binyamin, kept a family festival on the tenth of Av. One year the Ninth of Av fell on Shabbat and the fast was moved to Sunday, their festival day. They fasted part of the day but broke the fast before evening because of their festival.

answer.event: A brewer betrothed a woman with sediment from someone else's beer.
answer.turn: The owner found him and asked why he had not used the better, sharper sediment, which the brewer took as consent.
answer.outcome: Rava ruled that such a remark counts as consent only for teruma, so the brewer had no right to the sediment.
answer.summary: A brewer making beer for someone betrothed a woman using some of the beer sediment. The owner caught him and asked why he hadn't used the better sediment instead. The brewer asked Rava whether that showed consent, and Rava said such a remark counts as consent only in the case of teruma, not here.

answer.actor: an unnamed questioner and the people of Judea
answer.event: Following Rabbi Abba's suggestion, someone asked the people of Judea how two words in the mishna were spelled.
answer.turn: They answered that both spellings were in use.
answer.outcome: The question was settled as both versions being valid.
answer.summary: Rabbi Abba wished someone would ask the people of Judea, known for precise language, whether two mishnaic words were spelled with an alef or an ayin. Someone asked them, and they answered that some taught one spelling and some the other.
answer.missing: Hardly any event; it is mainly a reported answer about a textual reading.

answer.event: Rabbi Elazar missed the study hall one day and asked Rabbi Asi what had been taught.
answer.turn: Rabbi Asi told him Rabbi Yohanan ruled the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei.
answer.outcome: The report is given; the conversation continues as legal discussion.
answer.summary: Rabbi Elazar did not attend the study hall one day. Meeting Rabbi Asi, he asked what the Sages had said there, and Rabbi Asi reported Rabbi Yohanan's ruling that the law follows Rabbi Yosei.
answer.missing: Little beyond the transmission of a ruling; no real turn or ending.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabbi Hiyya
answer.event: When Rabbi fell ill, Rabbi Hiyya visited him and found him crying.
answer.turn: Rabbi Hiyya asked why he wept, since dying in tears is a bad omen.
answer.outcome: Rabbi answered that he was crying for the Torah and mitzvot he would no longer be able to fulfill.
answer.summary: When Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi fell ill, Rabbi Hiyya came to see him and found him crying. He asked why, reminding him of the tradition that dying while crying is a bad sign, and listing other omens at death. Rabbi replied that he was weeping over the Torah and commandments he would lose the chance to keep.

answer.event: Abdan's daughters-in-law rebelled against their husbands, and Rabbi sent two Sages to examine them.
answer.turn: When women pointed out their husbands approaching, they retorted, 'Let them be your husbands.'
answer.outcome: Rabbi declared there is no greater refusal than this.
answer.summary: The daughters-in-law of Abdan rebelled against their husbands, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi sent a pair of Sages to look into the matter. Other women said to them, 'Look, your husbands are coming,' and they answered, 'Let them be your husbands.' Rabbi ruled that there could be no clearer act of refusal.

answer.actor: Rabban Gamliel, Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva
answer.event: The Sages were sailing from Pelandarsin when their boat set out to sea on Shabbat, beyond the Shabbat limit.
answer.turn: Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya walked the whole boat while Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva stayed within four cubits.
answer.outcome: The two groups simply behaved differently; no further resolution.
answer.summary: Four Sages were traveling by ship from Pelandarsin when it sailed out to sea on Shabbat. Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya walked about the whole ship, while Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva, wanting to be strict with themselves, did not move beyond four cubits.
answer.missing: A turn or ending beyond the contrast in behavior.

answer.event: Rava asked Rav Nahman which tanna rejects retroactive designation even for rabbinic laws, citing a baraita.
answer.turn: Rav Nahman fell silent and gave no answer.
answer.outcome: The question went unanswered.
answer.summary: Rava challenged Rav Nahman to identify the tanna behind a baraita about choosing an eiruv recipient after nightfall. Rav Nahman stayed silent and said nothing.
answer.missing: Mostly legal argument; the only event is the unanswered question.

answer.actor: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
answer.event: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua conducted a halitza ceremony before five judges.
answer.outcome: The Gemara explains they did so to publicize the matter.
answer.summary: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua performed a halitza ceremony with five judges rather than three. The Gemara explains this was to make the event widely known, not because five were required.
answer.missing: A turn or developed narrative; it is a brief report of a practice.

answer.event: Doubting a ruling Rav Beruna attributed to Shmuel, Rabbi Elazar went to Shmuel's lodging and asked him directly.
answer.turn: Shmuel confirmed it, and Rabbi Elazar objected with Shmuel's own earlier statement.
answer.outcome: Shmuel fell silent.
answer.summary: Rav Beruna was teaching a ruling in Shmuel's name about alleyways. Rabbi Elazar doubted it and asked to be shown Shmuel's lodging, went there, and asked Shmuel, who confirmed it. Rabbi Elazar then confronted him with his own principle that eiruv law follows the wording of the mishna, and Shmuel had no answer.

answer.missing: Only a ruling about a mortar in Mar Shmuel's house and its reason; nothing turns.

answer.event: Rabbi Tarfon bent down so his mother could step on him to get into and out of bed, and boasted of it in the study hall.
answer.turn: The sages told him he had not reached even half the honor due her.
answer.outcome: They asked whether she had ever thrown his purse into the sea in front of him without his shaming her, deflating his boast.
answer.summary: Rabbi Tarfon honored his mother by letting her climb onto his back to get into and out of bed. He came and praised himself for this in the study hall. The sages answered that he had not reached even half of the honor owed to her: had she ever thrown his purse into the sea before his eyes without his embarrassing her?

answer.actor: a woman whose husband had died, and the people at Rabbi Yehuda's court
answer.event: A woman came to Rabbi Yehuda's court and the people there told her to lament her husband, tear her clothes and loosen her hair.
answer.turn: They coached her to show grief so that Rabbi Yehuda, who requires it, would believe her.
answer.summary: A woman came to Rabbi Yehuda's court to testify that her husband had died. The people there told her to lament him, tear her clothes and let down her hair, so that Rabbi Yehuda would accept her and allow her to remarry. The Gemara explains they were not teaching her to lie, since they held she could remarry anyway.
answer.missing: Whether Rabbi Yehuda permitted her to remarry.
A legal dispute citing, as evidence, that many were re-circumcised in Bar Kokhba's days; no individual event is told.

answer.actor: Rabbi Abbahu (or Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba), Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi
answer.event: Rabbi Abbahu sat and reported in Rabbi Yohanan's name that the halakha follows Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka.
answer.turn: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi turned their faces away in silent disagreement.
answer.outcome: They said nothing aloud, out of respect for Rabbi Abbahu's standing at Caesar's court.
answer.summary: Rabbi Abbahu sat and taught in Rabbi Yohanan's name that the halakha follows Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka. Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi, sitting opposite him, turned their faces away to show they disagreed with the report. Some say the speaker was Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba; Rav Pappa notes that only Rabbi Abbahu's ties to Caesar's court explain why they kept silent.
answer.missing: The incident is told as evidence and the speaker's identity is disputed; little resolution beyond the gesture.

answer.actor: a man who betrothed a woman conditionally, and the Sages
answer.event: A man betrothed a woman on a condition that was not fulfilled and then had relations with her.
answer.turn: The Sages could not declare the betrothal void.
answer.outcome: They could not release her without a bill of divorce.
answer.summary: Rav Kahana, citing Ulla, reports an actual case: a man betrothed a woman conditionally, the condition failed, and he later lived with her. The Sages found they had no power to let her go without a bill of divorce, so a divorce was required.
answer.missing: The incident is reported only in outline; names and details are absent.

answer.actor: a maidservant of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's household
answer.event: The maidservant immersed herself in a ritual bath and came out.
answer.turn: A bone was found between her teeth.
answer.outcome: Rabbi required her to immerse again.
answer.summary: A maidservant in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's household immersed for purity and came up out of the water. Then a bone was found stuck between her teeth. Rabbi ruled that the immersion did not count and made her immerse a second time.

answer.actor: Rav Yosef and his student Abaye
answer.event: Rav Yosef said he had never heard a certain halakha.
answer.turn: Abaye reminded him that Rav Yosef himself had taught it to them, along with the source and three lessons drawn from it.
answer.summary: When a teaching was cited, Rav Yosef said he had never heard it. His student Abaye told him he had taught it to them himself, on Rav Huna's ruling about a side post along an alleyway wall, and recited the three conclusions Rav Yosef had drawn from it. The English note explains Rav Yosef had forgotten his learning through illness.
answer.missing: Rav Yosef's reaction; the illness is supplied only by the translator's note.

answer.event: A woman's husband went overseas and she gave birth twelve months after he left.
answer.turn: Rava Tosfa'a ruled the child legitimate, presuming a delayed pregnancy.
answer.outcome: The child was declared fit (not a mamzer).
answer.summary: A woman's husband went abroad, and twelve months after he left she gave birth. Rava Tosfa'a ruled that the child was the husband's and legitimate, on the view that a pregnancy can be delayed. The Gemara then asks whose opinion that ruling followed.
answer.missing: The case is cited as a legal precedent; the people's reactions are absent.

answer.actor: a man whose betrothed died; Rav Nahman, Ulla, Avimei and Rav Hiyya bar Ami
answer.event: A man whose betrothed had died came before the sages, who told him to bury her or pay her marriage contract.
answer.turn: Rav Hiyya objected with a mishna that a betrothed man does not inherit his betrothed.
answer.summary: Rav Nahman, Ulla and Avimei bar Rav Pappi were sitting with Rav Hiyya bar Ami when a man came whose betrothed had died. They told him to bury her or pay her heirs her marriage contract. Rav Hiyya objected, citing a teaching that a betrothed husband does not inherit from her.
answer.missing: How the case was resolved.

answer.actor: Rav Yehuda, his father Rav Yehezkel, and Shmuel
answer.event: Rav Yehuda corrected the way his father Rav Yehezkel taught a mishna, and argued the point with him.
answer.turn: Shmuel rebuked Rav Yehuda for speaking to his father that way.
answer.outcome: Shmuel taught him the proper, indirect way to correct a parent.
answer.summary: Rav Yehezkel was teaching his son Rami a mishna about condemned criminals who became mixed up. His other son, Rav Yehuda, said: Father, do not teach it that way, and argued for his own version, answering his father's objection too. Later Shmuel told Rav Yehuda not to speak to his father like that, and taught that one should correct a parent only by quoting the verse, so the parent understands on his own.

answer.missing: A fragment of an exegetical argument about the Israelites eating after the omer; no narrated event.

answer.event: Rav Hisda praised Rav Hamnuna to Rav Huna, who asked to meet him.
answer.turn: Rav Huna saw Rav Hamnuna had no head-cloth and learned he was unmarried.
answer.outcome: Rav Huna turned his face away and told him not to see his face until he married.
answer.summary: Rav Hisda kept praising Rav Hamnuna to Rav Huna as a great man, so Rav Huna asked to have him sent over. When Rav Hamnuna came, Rav Huna noticed he did not wear a scholar's head-cloth, and Rav Hamnuna explained he was not married. Rav Huna turned his face away and told him not to come into his presence again until he married.

answer.actor: the sons of Rav Huna bar Avin
answer.event: They bought a maidservant for coins they did not have, leaving a piece of silver as collateral.
answer.turn: The maidservant's price rose and the sellers wanted to back out.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Ami ruled there had been no valid purchase.
answer.summary: The sons of Rav Huna bar Avin agreed to buy a maidservant for copper coins, but lacking the money they left a piece of silver as security. Later her value rose and the sellers wanted to cancel. They came before Rabbi Ami, who ruled that neither coins nor silver had been paid, so no sale had taken place.

answer.missing: A question put to Rabbi Eliezer and his answer, used to infer a legal view; no event.

answer.event: In Mar Shmuel's days there was some lentil bread, which he threw to his dog.
answer.turn: Even the dog would not eat it.
answer.summary: Some lentil bread was made in Mar Shmuel's time. He threw it to his dog, and even the dog refused to eat it. The Gemara cites this to question whether lentil bread is food.
answer.missing: Cited only as an objection; little beyond the single episode.

answer.event: A woman meant to invite her neighbor to come and eat milk.
answer.turn: Because of her slurred pronunciation she instead said, May a lioness eat you.
answer.summary: A Galilean woman wanted to say to her neighbor, Come, I will give you milk to eat. Because Galileans swallowed their guttural letters, what came out was, May a lioness eat you.
answer.missing: The neighbor's reaction; it is an illustrative anecdote.
Describes Mareimar's practice of closing Sura's alleyways with nets and his reason; no event that turns.

answer.event: Bar Shatya, who was sometimes insane, sold property.
answer.turn: Two witnesses said he sold it while sane and two others said while insane.
answer.outcome: Rav Ashi let the testimonies cancel and left the land in Bar Shatya's possession.
answer.summary: Bar Shatya, a man who had bouts of insanity, sold some land. One pair of witnesses testified that he was sane at the time, and another pair that he was insane. Rav Ashi ruled that the two pairs cancel each other out, so the land stays in Bar Shatya's possession.

answer.event: Seven teachings were said on Shabbat morning before Rav Hisda in Sura.
answer.turn: The same teachings were repeated that afternoon before Rava in Pumbedita, too far to have walked on Shabbat.
answer.summary: Seven teachings were stated one Shabbat morning before Rav Hisda in Sura. By the end of that same Shabbat they were repeated before Rava in Pumbedita, though the two cities were too far apart for anyone to travel between them on Shabbat. The Gemara goes on to ask who could have brought them.
answer.missing: Who carried the teachings; the context only speculates (Elijah or Yosef the demon).

answer.actor: the daughter-in-law of the house of bar Elyashiv
answer.event: She sued the orphans for her marriage-contract payment, and when they objected to her coming to court in house clothes, she put on all her garments.
answer.turn: By dressing in everything she owned, she brought all her clothes before the court, and Ravina ruled that a widow's clothes on her body are appraised.
answer.outcome: Ravina ruled per Rav that the clothes she wore were counted against her marriage-contract payment.
answer.summary: A widow in the bar Elyashiv family was taking the orphans to court to collect her marriage-contract money. The orphans said it was embarrassing for her to go in house clothes, so she went and dressed in all her garments. When they came before Ravina, he ruled that a widow's clothes on her person are appraised, so everything she had put on was counted toward her payment.

answer.actor: Rava and a woman whose husband died in a famine
answer.event: A woman testified to Rava that her husband died in a famine, and he cross-examined her about leaving him with a little flour.
answer.turn: She answered that the Master knows such a man could not survive, revealing she had not seen him die.
answer.outcome: Rava changed his view and ruled that famine is like war: such testimony is based on assumption.
answer.summary: Rava had thought a wife's report of her husband's death in a famine could be trusted. Then a woman came and said her husband had died of hunger; Rava asked whether she really thought he could survive on the bit of flour she left him. She replied that the Master knows nobody survives like that, showing she had only assumed his death. Rava then reversed himself and ruled that famine is like war.

answer.actor: Rabbi Ami, Rabbi Yirmeya and Rabbi Zerika
answer.event: A legal question about a slave who joined a foreign army was put to Rabbi Ami; Rabbi Zerika was sent to search his sources and found a related baraita.
answer.turn: The parallel was challenged, and Rabbi Ami then issued a public ruling.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Ami sent word to all Israel that the master may take the slave's value.
