answer.summary: Sages asked Rabbi Ami whether a master whose slave had run off to a foreign army could accept payment for him. Rabbi Yirmeya told Rabbi Zerika to go check his texts, and he found a teaching about a house seized by a gentile. After the comparison was questioned, Rabbi Ami sent out a ruling to all Israel permitting the master to take the slave's value.
answer.missing: The passage is mostly legal argument; the events are only the asking, the search and the sending of the ruling.

answer.event: Rav walked among sheaves of grain and saw them waving in the wind.
answer.turn: He told the sheaves that, wave as they might, business is better than farming.
answer.summary: Rav once walked between sheaves of grain in a field and saw them swaying in the wind. He addressed them: wave if you like, but trading brings more than you do.
answer.missing: The anecdote is a single remark with no further development; the rest is Rava's general saying.

answer.event: In Rabbi Pedat's house a beam so heavy that ten people were needed to lift it was placed against the door, and he did not object.
answer.turn: He explained that the beam has the status of a utensil.
answer.outcome: The practice was permitted.
answer.summary: Rabbi Pedat's household used to secure the door with a beam so heavy it took ten people to lift. He said nothing against it, explaining that the beam counted as a utensil and so could be used.
answer.missing: It is a description of a household practice and a ruling rather than a single event with a turn.

answer.event: While Rabbi Yehuda and others sat before Rabbi Tarfon, a yevama came to perform halitza.
answer.turn: Rabbi Tarfon instructed all present to call out 'He who had his shoe removed.'
answer.summary: Rabbi Yehuda recalled sitting with others before Rabbi Tarfon when a widow came to perform the halitza ceremony. Rabbi Tarfon told everyone present to respond together, 'He who had his shoe removed.'
answer.missing: The text does not say how the ceremony went or ended; it is cited as a source for a law.

answer.event: Rabbi Eliezer missed the study hall and asked Rabbi Asi what had been taught there.
answer.turn: Rabbi Asi reported that Rabbi Yohanan ruled like Rabbi Yosei, prompting Rabbi Eliezer to ask whether only one authority disagreed.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Asi confirmed it and cited a baraita in which Rabbi Meir alone disagrees.
answer.summary: One day Rabbi Eliezer did not go to the study hall. He met Rabbi Asi and asked what had been said there; Rabbi Asi told him Rabbi Yohanan had ruled like Rabbi Yosei. Rabbi Eliezer asked whether that meant a lone sage disagreed, and Rabbi Asi confirmed it by quoting a teaching.
answer.missing: It is essentially a conversation passing on a legal ruling.

answer.actor: Rav Aha bar Ya'akov and the students of Rav Huna
answer.event: Many of Rav Huna's students became impotent from holding back during his long lectures, and Rav Aha bar Ya'akov fell ill with a urinary disease.
answer.turn: He was hung from the cedar column of the study hall and a green substance came out of him.
answer.outcome: He was cured and alone of sixty elders did not become impotent.
answer.summary: Rav Giddel, Rav Helbo and Rav Sheshet all became impotent from sitting through Rav Huna's lengthy lectures without relieving themselves. Rav Aha bar Ya'akov caught a disease from the same cause; he was suspended from the cedar pillar of the study hall and a green fluid drained from him. He later said that of sixty elders present, he alone escaped impotence, because he applied the wisdom of that cure.

answer.event: Rav Safra challenged Rava over how Akistefon and Ardeshir could share a Shabbat limit when the Tigris separated them.
answer.turn: Rava went out and showed him the foundations of a wall submerged in the river, linking the cities.
answer.outcome: The question was answered by the physical evidence.
answer.summary: Rav Safra asked Rava how two cities on opposite banks of the Tigris could be treated as one for the Shabbat boundary, since the river put more than the allowed distance between them. Rava took him outside and showed him the remains of a city wall running into the river within seventy-odd cubits of the other town. The submerged wall joined the two cities.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yohanan and Rav Shemen bar Abba
answer.event: Rabbi Yohanan wondered why Rabbi Yishmael had not given sustenance to a woman whose husband went abroad.
answer.turn: Rav Shemen bar Abba told him Shmuel had explained the case as one where the husband was reported dead.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan was astonished at how far the Babylonians had gone in analysing it.
answer.summary: Rav Dimi reported that one such case came before Rabbi, who granted the wife support, and another before Rabbi Yishmael, who did not. Rabbi Yohanan was puzzled by Rabbi Yishmael's ruling. Rav Shemen bar Abba told him Shmuel in Babylonia had already explained it as a case where the husband was rumoured dead, and Rabbi Yohanan marvelled at their analysis.
answer.missing: The court cases themselves are only reported, not told; segment 4 is a variant version.

answer.actor: Rav Anan bar Tahalifa and Rav Ashi
answer.event: Each stood before his teacher when a pungent dish was served and was given some.
answer.turn: Each says that had he not been given a taste, he would have been endangered by craving.
answer.summary: Rav Anan bar Tahalifa recalled standing before Shmuel when a mushroom dish was brought, and said that if Shmuel had not shared it he would have been in danger. Rav Ashi told the same about turnip slices in vinegar served to Rav Kahana.
answer.missing: These are brief first-person recollections cited to support a rule, with no development.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi; the people of Bireta DeSatya
answer.event: On his deathbed Rabbi listed places in Babylonia, including Bireta DeSatya, whose people trapped fish on Shabbat.
answer.turn: Rabbi Ahai son of Rabbi Yoshiya excommunicated them, and they apostatized.
answer.outcome: That day they left Judaism; the final statement about Adda bar Ahava continues beyond the passage.
answer.summary: As Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi lay dying, he spoke of places in Babylonia: one full of Ammonites, one of mamzerim, one where two brothers swapped wives. Of Bireta DeSatya he said that on that very day its people had turned away from God: a fish pond overflowed on Shabbat, they caught the fish, Rabbi Ahai excommunicated them and they abandoned Judaism. He also said that in Akra DeAgma, Adda bar Ahava was that day being circumcised.
answer.missing: The Adda bar Ahava saying is completed only in the context segment.

answer.event: On his deathbed Rabbi made prophetic statements about places in Babylonia, including the apostasy of Bireta DeSatya after Shabbat fishing.
answer.turn: He announced that Adda bar Ahava was being circumcised that day and that Rav Yehuda had just been born.
answer.outcome: His death coincided with the birth of a successor.
answer.summary: As Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi was dying, he described places in Babylonia, telling how the people of Bireta DeSatya trapped fish on Shabbat, were excommunicated and apostatized that day. He added that Adda bar Ahava was being circumcised that day and that Rav Yehuda had just been born in Babylonia. The Gemara then explains this as showing that no righteous man dies before another is born.
answer.missing: The deathbed sayings are a list rather than one plot; segment 4 is commentary.

answer.event: Ten men carried a woman out on a bier, as though she were dead, and had intercourse with her.
answer.summary: There was an incident in which ten men took a woman out on a funeral bier as if she were a corpse and violated her. It is cited to show that even ten immoral men together do not restrain one another.
answer.missing: The incident is reported in one line, without any development or ending.

answer.actor: a man who betrothed a woman with a myrtle branch; Rav Aha bar Huna; Rav Yosef
answer.event: A man betrothed a woman in the marketplace with a myrtle branch, and Rav Aha bar Huna sent the case to Rav Yosef.
answer.turn: Rav Yosef ruled both ways at once: punish him and treat the betrothal as possibly valid.
answer.outcome: The man was to be flogged and the woman required a bill of divorce.
answer.summary: A man betrothed a woman in the market using a myrtle branch. Rav Aha bar Huna sent the case to Rav Yosef, who replied that the man should be flogged, as Rav did for marketplace betrothals, and the woman should get a divorce document, in case the branch was worth a peruta somewhere.

answer.event: Rav Yosef said he had never heard a certain ruling.
answer.turn: His student Abaye reminded him that he himself had taught it to them, and in what context.
answer.summary: Rav Yosef said he did not know a certain ruling about completing a fast. His student Abaye told him that he had taught it to them himself, and recounted the mishna and Rav's comment on which he had taught it.
answer.missing: Rav Yosef's illness and forgetting are supplied only by the translator's gloss; his response is not given.

answer.event: While Ameimar sat judging, a man removed a feather from his head; another man covered spittle in front of Mar Ukva.
answer.turn: Each man turned out to have a case to bring before the judge.
answer.outcome: Each judge disqualified himself from hearing the man's case.
answer.summary: Ameimar was sitting in judgment when a feather landed on his head and a man came and brushed it off. Asked what he was doing there, the man said he had a case, and Ameimar declared himself disqualified. Likewise a man covered spittle lying before Mar Ukva, said he had a case, and Mar Ukva disqualified himself.

answer.event: Ulla, who used to travel to the Land of Israel, died outside it, and Rabbi Elazar was told.
answer.turn: Rabbi Elazar lamented with a verse about dying in an unclean land; told the coffin was coming, he said burial after death is not the same.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Elazar held that being received by the Land while alive cannot be matched by burial there.
answer.summary: Ulla regularly went up to the Land of Israel, but he died abroad. When Rabbi Elazar heard, he cried, 'You, Ulla, shall die in an unclean land.' They told him Ulla's coffin was being brought for burial in Israel, but he answered that being absorbed by the Land in life is not like being absorbed after death.

answer.actor: a woman obligated to take an oath; Rav Beivai bar Abaye; Rav Pappi
answer.event: A woman owed an oath in Rav Beivai's court; her opponent asked that she swear in town, and she demanded a document of her rights first.
answer.turn: Rav Beivai ordered the document written, and Rav Pappi rebuked him for it.
answer.outcome: Rav Pappi mocked Rav Beivai's ruling as the foolish talk of an unfortunate family.
answer.summary: A woman was required to take an oath before Rav Beivai bar Abaye's court. Her opponent asked that she swear publicly in the town, hoping shame would make her confess; she agreed only if the court first wrote her a document of rights to be handed over once she swore. Rav Beivai told the court to write it, and Rav Pappi rebuked him, asking whether coming from an ill-fated family made him say ill-fated things.
